mistakes: Many candidates read single values off graphs and did not analyse long term trends.
Many noted the cause of a problem, but did not fully explain why it mattered.
Some answers gave too little developed evaluation, which often meant Level 1 for evaluation.
Most responses on aid described it in general terms and did not separate types of aid.
Some answers lacked a closing conclusion that follows from the evidence.
fix: Describe the long term trend in each variable, then explain how they relate.
For an assess question, say why the evidence matters and add a conclusion for the extra mark.
Use the evidence to judge which option works best, and separate short and long term.
Put a developed conclusion at the end. On one essay it could earn at least 4 of the 6 evaluation marks.
Explain how different types of aid change living standards, with reasoned links.

questions.issue: Many read off values at single points and did not discuss long run trends.
questions.fix: Describe the trends in both variables, then explain how they connect.

questions.topic: Assessing a monopoly's role in decline
questions.issue: Many mentioned power cuts without developing why they mattered. A significant number gave no conclusion.
questions.fix: Explain the effect and the general uncertainty, then give a conclusion from the evidence.

questions.issue: Weaker answers gave a brief conclusion, not a developed judgement.
questions.fix: Use a labelled diagram, compare policies and end with a developed, supported judgement.

questions.issue: Only stronger answers picked up the word always and tested when a monopoly might charge less.
questions.fix: Consider economies of scale and dynamic efficiency, and judge both prices and efficiency.

questions.topic: Fiscal policy and negative output gap
questions.issue: The term negative output gap may have put some candidates off. Only the strongest answers added the multiplier.
questions.fix: Know that a negative output gap is a deflationary gap, use a diagram, then evaluate with crowding out and long run alternatives.

questions.issue: Most described aid in general and did not compare types, so marks were low.
questions.fix: Compare types of aid and link each to living standards through reasoned steps.

quote.text: Candidates cannot gain credit for using the same analysis

takeaways: Read each question carefully before you write. On Paper 12, many lost marks on 1(c) by giving objectives when the question asked why objectives change.
Use a different detail from the case for each point. The same application or the same analysis twice only earns once.
In evaluation, make a decision, back it with a reason and say why it beats the other option. A bare decision or a summary does not count.
On Paper 22, never write the mirror of your first point to cover the second option. Give each option its own developed argument.
On Paper 22, when the case gives prices and costs, work through to profit for each option, label each figure correctly and base your recommendation on the results.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: The paper was accessible, and most candidates knew their content well.
In 1(d), most candidates knew non-financial motivators very well, and many explained them in context.
The questions on a recession, the secondary sector and cash inflows and outflows were well answered by most.
Location factors in 4(d) were well answered, and most candidates tied them to Suliman and his small online clothing business.
mistakes: Some definitions lacked precision. In 1(a), answers often mixed up added value with ideas such as profit margin.
Some candidates left out application or analysis, and some repeated knowledge instead of explaining how or why.
Many misread 1(c) and wrote objectives the business might set, not reasons its objectives changed.
Some answered a different topic, such as selection instead of recruitment, or advantages to the host country instead of to the company.
Many part (e) answers gave no decision, and most of those that did could not support it with reasons.
fix: Learn each key term in full, and do not reuse the word you are defining.
Pick a fresh detail from the stem for each point, and do not reuse anything the question itself states.
Develop a point by explaining its effect on the business. Do not just add a new point.
Check the exact focus of the question, such as recruitment methods or advantages to the business, before you start.
End every part (e) with a clear choice, the main reason behind it, and a line on why the other option falls short.

questions.issue: Most linked it to selling price but could not bring in the cost of raw materials. Some listed ways to raise it.
questions.fix: Define it as the gap between the selling price and the cost of the bought in materials.

questions.issue: Poorly answered. Many listed objectives instead of reasons for a change.
questions.fix: Give reasons such as objectives already achieved or a change in demand or competition, linked to the bakery.

questions.issue: The most common mistake was writing about selection. Others mixed up job adverts with product adverts.
questions.fix: Name a real method, such as a recruitment agency or a newspaper advert, and explain an advantage of each.

questions.issue: Some repeated hats as the application for both points, and some wrote what happens if the business ignores the law.
questions.fix: Say what the business might have to change, such as its production methods or materials, with a new detail each time.

questions.topic: Why a business uses market research
questions.issue: Vague claims such as ensuring success were not credited, and some listed research methods instead.
questions.fix: Explain how each reason helps, such as finding customer needs to develop suitable products, then judge which matters more.

questions.topic: Uses of a cash flow forecast
questions.issue: Challenging for most. Some thought it measures profit or working capital, or mixed it up with an income statement.
questions.fix: Explain uses such as backing a loan application or spotting a shortfall early so the business can act.

questions.issue: A common mistake was working out revenue or contribution instead.
questions.fix: Take break-even output away from current sales and give the answer in units.

questions.issue: Some gave advertising methods, and some used the word shop as application, which the question already gives.
questions.fix: Give methods such as discounts or buy one get one free, each tied to a different detail from the stem or table.

papers.title: Case study
well: Most candidates came well prepared, and plenty of scripts scored highly.
Reasons why governments support new businesses were well answered.
The majority knew that a stronger currency makes imported ingredients cheaper.
Many calculated gross profit and profit correctly to compare the two meals.
mistakes: In 1(b), the health and safety effects were often stated briefly rather than explained, which kept answers in the lower band.
Some found segmentation and a rise in the exchange rate harder, and weaker answers said imports would cost more.
In 3(b) many explained new technology well, then just mirrored it for the existing equipment.
Retained profit answers showed very good knowledge but were often poorly applied.
Weaker answers labelled profit as gross profit or revenue, or made assumptions the data did not support.
fix: Say how a decision changes the business, for example its costs or its sales, not just that it changes.
Give a different case detail for each advantage and disadvantage, such as the 90 per cent of imported ingredients.
Treat each option on its own merits. Do not assume existing equipment is old when the case says it works well.
Label every calculated figure correctly and only use claims the appendix supports.
In a recommendation, back your choice, tie it to AF, and explain what made the other option weaker.

questions.issue: Reasons were often repeated, not explained, and some weaker answers explained how governments help instead of why.
questions.fix: State the reason, then its effect, such as more jobs bringing the unemployment rate down.

questions.topic: Effects of three changes to employment law
questions.issue: Health and safety points were often brief. Weaker answers said the 50 hour limit would not matter, thinking staff only needed to work 40 hours.
questions.fix: Use the figures in the case, and explain knock on effects such as missing orders in busy periods.

questions.issue: Some second benefits just rephrased the first, and weaker answers wrote about market research.
questions.fix: Develop each benefit, such as a higher price where the segment has little competition, giving a higher margin.

questions.issue: Weaker answers called penetration pricing a high price, and many conclusions did not say whether the mix was suitable.
questions.fix: Remember penetration means a low price, and end by judging whether the whole mix suits the business.

questions.issue: Weaker answers said imports would be dearer, and some wrote about exporting meals, which did not fit the business.
questions.fix: Explain that imported ingredients get cheaper, lowering costs, which could allow lower prices or higher profit.

questions.topic: New technology against more existing equipment
questions.issue: Mirror arguments limited marks, so only better candidates reached Level 3.
questions.fix: Use case details such as the 10 skilled employees and the two equipment costs, and justify your rejection.

questions.topic: Retained profit as a source of finance
questions.issue: Knowledge was very good, but application was generally more limited.
questions.fix: Tie each advantage and disadvantage to the business, not to firms in general.

questions.issue: Some stopped at total revenue and total costs, or gave simple comparisons such as one price being higher.
questions.fix: Go on to profit for each meal, then base your recommendation on those results.

quote.text: Easy marks are frequently missed due to not reading instructions

takeaways: Follow the instructions to the letter: amounts not ticks, two decimal places when asked, and stop where the question stops.
Every question is compulsory, so revise the whole syllabus. On Paper 22, club accounts caused more trouble than the accounts of other organisations.
Write a working beside every calculation. Without one, a wrong figure scores nothing at all.
Label figures with proper account names. Avoid shortcuts such as GP, COGS and BBD.
In the five mark advice questions, use the facts in the scenario on both sides and finish with a firm recommendation.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates had a sound grip on bookkeeping and scored on a good share of the paper.
Most candidates answered the opening questions on the accountant's role and the accounting equation correctly.
Many picked the correct statement about depreciation and the correct inventory valuation, and many were right on the incomplete records profit.
mistakes: Some found the entry for a loss for the year challenging.
Some thought a statement of account would show trade discount.
Some did not notice that one depreciation option was about current assets.
Some worked out inventory from the combined cost and net realisable value totals.
Some seemed to find the question on which error overstates gross profit slightly challenging.
fix: Give each question your full attention before you mark an answer.
Apply the lower of cost and net realisable value to each line of inventory separately.
Trace how an error changes cost of sales before you decide its effect on gross profit.
Keep receipts and payments for a club in the receipts and payments account, not in the income and expenditure account.

questions.topic: Loss for the year in the capital account
questions.issue: Some found this challenging and chose a wrong option.
questions.fix: A loss reduces capital, so it is a debit in the capital account and a credit in the income statement.

questions.topic: What a statement of account shows
questions.issue: Many answered correctly, though some included trade discount.
questions.fix: Trade discount is taken off before anything is recorded, so it never shows on the statement.

questions.issue: The cash book balance had to be adjusted for timing items, and the bank had also charged interest in error.
questions.fix: Start from the cash book balance, add the unpresented cheques, take off the uncredited deposits, then take off the interest charged in error.

questions.issue: Many were right, but some used the combined totals for cost and net realisable value.
questions.fix: Value each type at the lower of its own cost and net realisable value, then add the two.

questions.issue: Some seemed to find this slightly challenging.
questions.fix: Leaving out opening inventory makes cost of sales too low, so gross profit comes out too high.

questions.issue: The amount left for the dividend had to be found before the percentage.
questions.fix: Take the general reserve transfer and the interim dividend away from profit, then show what is left as a percentage of share capital.

questions.issue: Many chose correctly, but some found it challenging.
questions.fix: Credit sales are 90 per cent of all sales, so find total sales before applying the 30 per cent margin.

questions.issue: Candidates had to work out expenses as a share of revenue from two margins.
questions.fix: Take the profit margin from the gross margin. The lowest result controls overheads best.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates had a good understanding of double entry and used it well.
Most answered the first two questions, on the purpose of bookkeeping and on definitions, correctly.
Most worked out the music club concert profit without trouble.
mistakes: Some found the suspense account question challenging.
Some credited money from a written off debtor to the irrecoverable receivables account.
Many chose a wrong option for the insurance charge.
Some put the purchase of new furniture in a club's income and expenditure account.
Some appeared to struggle with finding profit from capital and with the acid test question, and others got the purchases calculation wrong.
fix: Read the whole question first, then choose.
Spread an expense over the months at each rate before adding.
Learn which figures make up return and capital employed.
Use the capital equation to find a missing profit.

questions.topic: Effect of errors on the trial balance
questions.issue: Two items were on the wrong side, so each one moved the totals by twice its amount.
questions.fix: Double each misplaced amount and net the effects to find how far the totals differ.

questions.topic: Entry that opened the suspense account
questions.issue: Some found this challenging and picked a wrong option.
questions.fix: Decide the side of each correcting entry, then work back to the opening suspense balance.

questions.topic: Cash from a debt already written off
questions.issue: Most debited the bank, but some credited irrecoverable receivables.
questions.fix: The credit goes to the debts recovered account.

questions.issue: Some got it right, but many chose a wrong option.
questions.fix: Charge nine months at the first rate and three months at the new rate.

questions.topic: Sports club income and expenditure items
questions.issue: Some thought new furniture belonged there.
questions.fix: Furniture is a capital purchase. Depreciation and subscriptions due for the year belong there.

questions.topic: Profit for the year from capital
questions.issue: This appeared to trouble some candidates, although a significant number got it right.
questions.fix: Opening capital plus profit less drawings gives closing capital. Rearrange it to find profit.

questions.issue: Candidates needed to know what counts as return and as capital employed.
questions.fix: Return is profit before interest. Capital employed is equity plus debentures.

questions.topic: Fall in the liquid (acid test) ratio
questions.issue: Some found this slightly challenging and picked a wrong option.
questions.fix: Ask how each change moves current assets less inventory and current liabilities.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Candidates with a good grasp of the syllabus earned high grades, and most scripts were well presented.
Many scored highly on the petty cash book, and most got at least half the marks for the supplier ledger account.
Most earned at least half the marks on sorting capital and revenue expenditure.
Many gave good statements of financial position and gave sound advice on shares against a bank loan.
mistakes: In a few scripts, words and figures were hard to read or had been written over.
Asked for two reasons for a provision for doubtful debts, most named prudence and often expanded on it instead of giving a second reason.
In the suspense account, some posted the two right errors but added many items that did not affect the trial balance.
In the manufacturing account, some put office costs in factory overheads or took overheads away from prime cost.
Many thought giving up cash would harm liquidity, and some wrote about trading on credit instead.
fix: Show every calculation, so some marks are possible even when the answer is wrong.
Give two different reasons when the question asks for two.
Add factory overheads to prime cost, and label cost of material used, prime cost and cost of production.
Answer the exact choice the trader is facing in an advice question.

questions.issue: Some said bank charges would start, though the trader already paid them, and many wrongly linked it to liquidity.
questions.fix: Weigh safety and time saved against customers and suppliers who may still want cash.

questions.topic: Reasons for a provision for doubtful debts
questions.issue: Most gave prudence, often expanding it instead of moving to another reason. Preventing fraud was not accepted.
questions.fix: Give prudence as one reason and a genuinely different second reason.

questions.topic: Provision for depreciation of motor vehicles
questions.issue: Challenging for many. Errors included adding the cost price and leaving out depreciation on the vehicle sold.
questions.fix: Bring in the depreciation on the disposal from 2(b), and check the charge for the year.

questions.issue: Some entered the two right errors but added many others, losing the own figure mark.
questions.fix: Post only the errors that affected the trial balance totals.

questions.issue: Errors included leaving out profit or opening capital, adding the suspense account and reversing adjustments.
questions.fix: Start with opening capital, add the corrected profit, then take off drawings. Show each correction to profit with its sign.

questions.issue: Some lost marks on detail, such as non factory items in overheads and missing labels.
questions.fix: Keep office expenses and machinery cost out, and label each subtotal.

questions.topic: Turning office space into factory space
questions.issue: Many gave only one advantage and one disadvantage, and did not always see that extra output might not sell.
questions.fix: Give two of each and ask whether the extra output can actually be sold.

questions.issue: Many earned full marks, but some included non-current or total assets or did not show a ratio.
questions.fix: Use current assets less inventory over current liabilities, and write the answer as a ratio to 1.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Discussion questions were on the whole handled well, and many candidates came ready for the financial statements questions.
Scores of 9 or more on the cash book were common.
The journal question was generally handled well, with the common slips in items three and four.
Most scored full marks on the partnership appropriation account, and most earned three of the four marks on the trading account.
mistakes: Weaker cash books included credit purchases, which involve no cash.
In the journal, loan and loan interest were doubled, and an unneeded suspense entry was made.
Common slips in the income and expenditure account were using bank receipts as income and not adjusting insurance for the prepayment.
The accumulated fund was often described as capital.
In the gross margin, some used revenue instead of net revenue.
fix: Leave credit purchases out of the cash book.
Start the income and expenditure account from the income worked out in the subscriptions account.
Put fittings at cost and their depreciation provision on opposite sides of the trial balance.
Show cost of sales in the right order and include carriage inwards.

questions.issue: The capital received was put on both sides or called drawings, and narratives were not account names.
questions.fix: Record the capital once on the debit side, and use account names for every entry.

questions.issue: Many just said the debt is an expense, which did not show how it meets the principle.
questions.fix: Say that writing off the debt stops profit and assets being overstated.

questions.issue: Most earned one mark, but the second needed the effect of ignoring the principle.
questions.fix: Add that mixing in the owner's spending would understate profit or overstate capital.

questions.issue: Common mistakes were using bank receipts as income and adding the closing bank balance.
questions.fix: Use the subscriptions income from 3(a), adjust insurance for the prepayment and include subscriptions written off.

questions.issue: A small number used initials, deducted interest on drawings or added interest on capital wrongly.
questions.fix: Use full names, add interest on drawings and take off interest on capital.

questions.issue: Many repeated items from the question, and loan interest was given without saying whose loan.
questions.fix: Give items not already listed, each stated precisely.

questions.issue: Entries were reversed or put on the same side, and both inventory figures were included.
questions.fix: Enter only the opening inventory, and add a suspense balance if the totals still differ.

questions.issue: Most missed that the competitor owns its premises and has a similar gross margin.
questions.fix: Use the scenario: similar gross margins are expected, so look at rent and other expenses.

quote.text: close inspection of each word in the questions

takeaways: Read every word of the question, not just its topic. Causes are not consequences, and a question about firms is not about consumers.
Treat the source as your evidence in Section A. The guidance before Question 1 tells you to refer to it, and the questions are written to need it.
Develop each point you make. Naming a factor without saying what it does leaves marks behind.
Plan your time by the marks. The Paper 23 report suggests about 45 minutes for Question 1 and 90 minutes for the three optional questions.
When a question only asks you to draw a diagram, draw and label it carefully and do not write an explanation.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 2, 3, 17, 19 and 25 were answered correctly by 75 per cent or more of the candidates.
mistakes: Questions 5, 9, 15, 16 and 18 were answered correctly by fewer than half the candidates.
Almost a third chose increase in demand for a price fall, which the report calls confusing a movement along the curve with a shift.
43 per cent picked a rise in farmworkers' wages as the cause of a movement up the supply curve, more than chose the right answer.
Over half picked average total cost (29 per cent) or total variable cost (23 per cent) when average variable cost was asked for.
Just over half missed the one pair that was purely monetary policy, and the report suggests they may not have noticed that word.
fix: Read each item through carefully before you choose.
Only a change in the good's own price moves you along a curve. Any other change shifts it.
Practise reading numbers off cost curves, starting with fixed cost at zero output.

questions.issue: 44 per cent chose correctly. 31 per cent picked increase in demand, mixing up a movement with a shift.
questions.fix: A move down the demand curve after a price fall is an extension, not an increase.

questions.issue: 39 per cent chose correctly, while 43 per cent picked higher farm wages.
questions.fix: Higher wages raise costs and shift supply. Higher incomes raise demand, which moves the market along supply.

questions.issue: 35 per cent chose correctly. 29 per cent gave average total cost and 23 per cent total variable cost.
questions.fix: Subtract the fixed cost from total cost, then divide by output.

questions.issue: 48 per cent chose correctly, and 24 per cent chose external economies of scale.
questions.fix: All factors doubled, so it is the long run. Output rising by less than double shows diseconomies of scale.

questions.issue: 47 per cent chose correctly. The report suggests the rest may have missed the word monetary.
questions.fix: Pick the option where both measures are monetary, and rule out any tax or spending measure.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 1, 3, 4, 12, 13, 15, 20, 23 and 27 were answered correctly by 80 per cent or more of the candidates.
Only two questions were answered correctly by fewer than half the candidates.
mistakes: More candidates said a rise in indirect taxes would lower inflation than chose the right answer.
Only 41 per cent saw that cutting an import quota helps a current account deficit. The report says quota changes can cause confusion.
fix: Think about what a tax does to prices as well as to government revenue.
A cut in a quota lets in fewer imports, so spending on imports falls.

questions.issue: 33 per cent were right, and 36 per cent picked lower inflation.
questions.fix: Higher indirect taxes push prices up, but they bring in revenue that helps reduce a budget deficit.

questions.issue: 41 per cent were right, and 30 per cent chose lowering income tax.
questions.fix: Reducing an import quota lowers spending on imports and helps reduce the deficit.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 2, 7, 11, 12, 23 and 30 were answered correctly by 85 per cent or more, and the mean mark was slightly higher than in June 2022.
mistakes: Only Questions 14 and 17 were answered correctly by fewer than 40 per cent.
Only about a third linked staying small to diseconomies of scale at low output.
Only about a quarter picked the one true public good, and more chose railways than the right answer.
fix: Ask whether each cost effect would push a firm to grow or to stay small.
Test each option: can people be charged and kept out, and does one person's use reduce what others get?

questions.issue: 34 per cent were right, and 29 per cent chose external diseconomies of scale at high output.
questions.fix: Internal economies of scale encourage growth. Diseconomies of scale give a reason to stay small.

questions.issue: 26 per cent were right, and 35 per cent chose railways.
questions.fix: Education, healthcare and rail travel can all be charged for, so only national defence is a public good.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Most candidates laid out their answers clearly, so they were easy to follow.
Nearly all found at least two substitutes for coal in the source.
Most explained how better education changes demand for cigarettes and fresh fruit, and many split relative from absolute poverty.
Most gave two valid reasons why death rates differ, and the life expectancy question was answered well.
mistakes: Some named a factor but did not develop it, and the report warns this can cost a lot of marks.
In 1(f) and 1(g), many did not use the source material.
A common error was saying population size changes the death rate, which is measured per 1,000 people.
Some thought people finding work adds to the labour force, mixing it up with employment.
Many could not explain why inflation rates differ between countries.
fix: Avoid jumping between questions, and number every answer clearly.
Only cross out work when you have made a second attempt.
Explain how a cause works, for example that a higher birth rate only adds to the labour force in the long run.
Name the actual taxes behind a rise in tax revenue, such as income tax or sales tax.

questions.issue: Slightly fewer than half were right. The most common error used the total population.
questions.fix: Divide the unemployed by the labour force and multiply by 100 to get a percentage.

questions.issue: Only a few showed the ceiling below equilibrium with the shortage. Many shifted a curve instead.
questions.fix: Leave the curves where they are, draw the price line below equilibrium and mark the excess demand.

questions.topic: Whether a bigger coal industry benefits Australia
questions.issue: There were some good answers, but weaker ones were one sided or listed factors without development.
questions.fix: Develop reasons it would help, such as jobs and exports, and reasons it might not, such as pollution.

questions.issue: The wording was often wrong, and a few gave characteristics such as portable instead.
questions.fix: Learn the exact names of the functions, such as medium of exchange.

questions.issue: Weaker answers just said tax rates rose, and a few wrote about effects instead of causes.
questions.fix: Link each cause, such as more employment, to the tax it would raise.

questions.topic: Labour productivity and a current account surplus
questions.issue: Relatively few explained why the extra output would raise exports, and a small number wrote about the budget.
questions.fix: Explain why exports rise, such as better quality or lower prices, and say what may happen to imports.

questions.topic: Long term unemployment and finding work
questions.issue: Weaker answers leaned too heavily on lost skills and reused the same point several ways.
questions.fix: Cover other factors too, such as retraining costs, motivation, age and the state of the economy.

questions.topic: Whether a government should encourage mergers
questions.issue: The government angle was not understood by most, and weaker answers listed types of merger.
questions.fix: Weigh gains such as economies of scale and competitiveness against less competition and the risk of monopoly.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: There were some excellent scripts, with few question parts left blank.
Most found 35 per cent of the population correctly.
Reasons linked to occupational and geographical mobility were generally well answered.
Most identified influences on choosing a bank, and the reasons for tariffs on imports were generally well answered.
mistakes: The examiners again saw production and productivity used as if they meant the same thing.
The (b) parts were rather hard for some candidates.
Some gave GDP per head when the source pointed to real GDP as the growth measure.
Some wrote about why firms want higher prices, not why a merger may lead to them.
Some (d) answers stated points without analysis, which keeps them in Level 1.
fix: Think through an answer before you start to write.
Answer only the side the question asks for, such as benefits of more bank lending.
In a (d) answer, give both sides and analyse at least one in depth.
Use the demand for and supply of labour to explain why one group earns more.

questions.topic: Cheaper rail transport and the market for car transport
questions.issue: Some wrote long explanations nobody asked for, mixed up the curves or mislabelled the axes.
questions.fix: Label both axes and both curves, and mark the original and new equilibrium.

questions.topic: GDP per head and internet access
questions.issue: Some described the table but did not pull out the relationship.
questions.fix: State the link, support it with a country from the table, and point out an exception.

questions.topic: Why a merger may raise prices
questions.issue: Some wrote about why firms want higher prices.
questions.fix: Explain causes such as more market power or diseconomies of scale.

questions.issue: Some were confused about what land is and wrote about changes in its use.
questions.fix: Use examples such as finding new natural resources for quantity and using fertilisers for quality.

questions.topic: Whether to prevent a rise in unemployment
questions.issue: Some wrote about how to reduce unemployment instead.
questions.fix: Weigh the harm unemployment does against reasons it may not be a problem, such as temporary frictional unemployment.

questions.issue: Some confused a rise in the exchange rate with a fall.
questions.fix: Explain changes in the demand for and supply of the currency, such as hot money flows.

questions.issue: A number thought the opportunity cost of exporting was importing.
questions.fix: The goods exported could have been sold at home instead.

questions.issue: Some mentioned years of training without linking it to low supply.
questions.fix: Tie each factor to the demand for or supply of these workers.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Fewer candidates broke the paper's instructions than in recent sessions, and most labelled their answers clearly.
The majority worked out GDP per head correctly, and most identified the two external costs in 1(b).
Most named two costs of a firm and two roles of commercial banks, and most named two challenges for small firms.
Understanding of opportunity cost was generally good.
mistakes: Some ran out of time after very long answers to 1(g) and 1(h), leaving short optional answers.
A small minority answered every optional question, and others answered only three questions in total.
Those who chose 4(b) often wrote about the consequences of a recession when the question asked for causes.
Some confused commercial banks with central banks, and others confused immigration with emigration.
Conclusions that only repeated earlier points added nothing.
fix: Answer all of Question 1 and then exactly three optional questions.
Check every number for size. An income per person of a few dollars or billions of dollars should look wrong.
Build the analyse questions on economic theory, such as demand and supply.
Only write a conclusion that adds something new to the discussion.

questions.topic: Impact on a cow farmer's profits
questions.issue: Answers split between those who understood profit and those with only a vague idea.
questions.fix: Profit is revenue minus costs. Show that revenue falls because sales fall.

questions.topic: Two plans to reduce external costs
questions.issue: Some explained the result, less environmental damage, instead of the plan itself.
questions.fix: Explain what each plan does: ending imports of petrol powered cars by 2032 and limiting the number of cows each farmer keeps.

questions.topic: Share of world GDP and of CO2 emissions
questions.issue: Weaker answers wrote at length but ignored the data, and a number left it blank.
questions.fix: State the positive relationship, prove it with two countries and name the exception.

questions.topic: Clean and green exports and macroeconomic aims
questions.issue: Answers that discussed green issues in general lacked focus.
questions.fix: Use the four aims as your structure: current account, growth, employment and inflation.

questions.topic: Job losses from a carbon neutral economy
questions.issue: Many ignored the job losses in the question and discussed the change in general.
questions.fix: Weigh poverty and lost output and taxes against unemployment that may be temporary.

questions.issue: Many wrote about the incomes of people within a country.
questions.fix: Explain what drives national output, such as education, investment and natural resources.

questions.topic: Causes of a fall in demand for Chinese food
questions.issue: Some thought it meant food imported from China, and many answers were general.
questions.fix: Use demand theory: a cheaper substitute, lower incomes or a change in tastes.

questions.issue: A clear answer was rare. Many thought private benefits go to the private sector and external ones to the public sector.
questions.fix: Private benefits go to the buyer or seller. External benefits go to a third party.

quote.text: productivity does not have the same meaning as production

takeaways: In Section A, build every answer on the source material. On Paper 21 many ignored it in 1(f) and 1(g) and scored low or nothing.
A named factor earns little on its own. Say what it leads to, because undeveloped points cost marks on Papers 21 and 22.
Answer the exact question set. Candidates wrote about effects when asked for causes, about reducing unemployment when asked whether to prevent a rise, or about a fall when the question was a rise.
Keep key terms apart: production and productivity, a budget deficit and a current account deficit, demand and supply elasticity.
In the (d) essays, argue both sides with real economics and take at least one side into depth. Points that are only stated stay in Level 1.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 1, 2, 10, 14, 19 and 24 were answered correctly by 75 per cent or more of candidates.
mistakes: The mean mark was lower than in June 2022, and six questions were answered correctly by fewer than half.
Two in five chose increase in demand for a price fall, which the report calls mixing up a movement along the curve with a shift.
Almost half (48 per cent) picked higher farm wages as the cause of a movement up the supply curve, but wages shift supply.
Well over half picked average total cost (34 per cent) or total variable cost (25 per cent) when average variable cost was asked for.
Nearly two thirds missed the one purely monetary pair, and the report suggests they may have overlooked that word.
fix: Read each item slowly before you shade an answer, especially the words only and not.
A price change moves you along a curve. Anything else shifts it.
Find fixed cost where output is zero, take it from total cost, then divide by output for average variable cost.
Learn which measures are monetary, such as interest rates, and which are fiscal, such as taxes.

questions.issue: 34 per cent were right. 40 per cent chose increase in demand, mixing up a movement along the curve with a shift.
questions.fix: A move along the demand curve after a price fall is an extension. A shift outwards is an increase.

questions.issue: 29 per cent were right. 48 per cent chose higher farm wages, which shifts supply.
questions.fix: Higher incomes raise demand, which moves the market up along the supply curve.

questions.topic: Average variable cost from a total cost curve
questions.issue: 33 per cent were right. Slightly more, 34 per cent, chose average total cost, and 25 per cent chose total variable cost.
questions.fix: Take away the fixed cost shown at zero output, then divide what is left by the units produced.

questions.issue: 41 per cent were right, and 36 per cent chose external economies of scale.
questions.fix: Every input doubled, so this is the long run, yet output only went from 100 to 150. Output growing by less than the inputs is diseconomies of scale.

questions.issue: 36 per cent were right. The report suggests others may have missed that only monetary measures were wanted.
questions.fix: Rule out any option that contains a fiscal measure before you choose.

questions.issue: 45 per cent were right. The report suggests the 28 per cent choosing C may have read it as a question about higher inflation.
questions.fix: At full employment, extra spending pushes prices up in the short run. A more skilled workforce makes low inflation more likely later.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Questions 1, 3, 4, 12, 13, 15, 20 and 27 were answered correctly by 80 per cent or more of candidates, and the mean mark rose from June 2022.
mistakes: Questions 17, 21 and 30 were answered correctly by fewer than 40 per cent.
Almost a third chose lower inflation as the aim of higher indirect taxes, when such taxes tend to push prices up.
Over half read more into GDP data than it showed, choosing a rise in the growth rate.
Only 30 per cent picked lowering import quotas to help a current account deficit, and more chose lowering income tax.
fix: Ask what a tax change does to prices as well as to government revenue.
Only conclude what the data shows. Without population figures you cannot judge growth per head.
Check which way a policy moves imports and exports before you judge its effect on the current account.

questions.topic: Why a government raises indirect taxes
questions.issue: 36 per cent were right. 30 per cent chose lower inflation, but higher indirect taxes tend to raise prices.
questions.fix: Higher indirect taxes raise revenue, which helps to reduce a budget deficit.

questions.issue: 27 per cent were right. 52 per cent chose a rise in the growth rate, which the data did not show.
questions.fix: Real GDP rose each year, so there was growth. It rose by 10 billion, then only 4 billion, so the growth rate did not increase.

questions.issue: 30 per cent were right, and 37 per cent chose lowering income tax.
questions.fix: A lower quota means fewer goods may come in, so less is spent on imports and the deficit shrinks.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Most candidates set out their answers in a clear and logical order.
In 1(b), almost every candidate picked out two or more of the coal substitutes the source named.
The question on how education changes demand for cigarettes and fruit was well answered.
The question on government spending to raise life expectancy was answered well.
mistakes: A major reason some scored lower was naming a relevant factor and leaving it undeveloped.
The source was ignored by many in 1(f) and 1(g), and many 1(h) answers overlooked the fact file.
In 1(d), the main reason for so few correct answers was writing about elasticity of demand instead of supply.
Only a few could explain a public good, and many called it a good the government provides.
Quite a few said a rise in the exchange rate makes exports cheaper.
fix: After naming each factor, say what it does, such as making supply more inelastic.
In Section A, quote the table or fact file and pick out the relationship it shows.
Leave a gap between answers, and cross out only when a second attempt replaces the first.
Define a public good as non rival and non excludable, which is why private firms would not supply it.
Remember a higher exchange rate makes exports dearer and imports cheaper.

questions.issue: Just under half got the rate right. Dividing by the whole population was the most common slip.
questions.fix: Put the working population on the bottom of the fraction, not everyone in the country, and turn the result into a percentage.

questions.topic: Economy of scale for a coal mining firm
questions.issue: Quite a few named financial or purchasing economies with no support in the source, or found the feature but not its name.
questions.fix: Pick the feature in the source, such as specialist staff, and name the economy it shows.

questions.topic: Price elasticity of supply of coal
questions.issue: Correct answers were limited. Many wrote about demand, or named an influence without saying its effect.
questions.fix: Name the influence from the source and say it makes supply more inelastic or more elastic.

questions.issue: Most drew the basic diagram, but only a few added the maximum price and the shortage it creates. Many moved a curve down to a new equilibrium.
questions.fix: Draw a horizontal line below equilibrium and mark the gap between demand and supply at that price.

questions.topic: Whether large coal producers are net exporters
questions.issue: Few used the table, and very few saw that the two largest producers used more coal than they produced.
questions.fix: Compare output with consumption for each country and state the pattern, then any exception.

questions.topic: Whether Australia will have a budget deficit in 2026
questions.issue: Many looked only at coal and ignored the fact file. A few mixed it up with a balance of payments deficit.
questions.fix: Use the fact file figures, such as unemployment and GDP, on both sides of the argument.

questions.topic: Effects of a rise in the foreign exchange rate
questions.issue: Quite a few said exports would get cheaper and imports dearer, then followed that wrong path.
questions.fix: Exports become dearer, so export revenue tends to fall unless demand is inelastic, while imports get cheaper.

questions.topic: Points inside and on a PPC
questions.issue: Many found it challenging. Answers covered efficiency but not the output achieved, and diagrams were often off the point.
questions.fix: Inside the curve, resources are wasted and output is below what is possible. On it, output is at its maximum.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: The best scripts applied relevant economics to every question part.
The causes in 1(b) and the reasons in 1(d) were generally well answered.
There were many strong answers on oil and living standards in 1(g), and 1(h) was generally well answered.
Answers on reasons for tariffs showed good knowledge of infant and declining industries, and a fairly high share understood dumping.
mistakes: Some candidates struggled with the (b) parts this session.
Production and productivity were still being swapped, a slip earlier reports have also raised.
Some confused a budget deficit with a current account deficit.
Some (d) answers stayed general, with little economic theory in them.
Some answered a different question, such as reducing unemployment when asked whether to prevent a rise.
fix: Plan each answer in your head, or in a short note, before writing it.
Level 3 needs two sides with depth on one or more of them. One sided answers or stated points sit lower.
When asked only to draw a diagram, just draw it with labelled axes and both equilibriums.
Explain why each change happens, not only that it happens.

questions.topic: Number of people living in poverty
questions.issue: Most were right, but some misplaced a digit and others used the optimum population figure.
questions.fix: Use the actual population size, and check the size of your answer.

questions.issue: Some gave GDP per head, unemployment or inflation instead of real GDP.
questions.fix: Economic growth is a rise in total output, so pick real GDP from the source.

questions.topic: Cheaper rail travel and demand for car transport
questions.issue: Time went on explaining a diagram that only had to be drawn. Even some strong candidates swapped the curves, and a number got the axis labels wrong.
questions.fix: Rail is a substitute that got cheaper, so shift demand for car transport left and mark the old and new equilibrium.

questions.topic: GDP per head and internet access
questions.issue: Weaker answers retold the figures, missing for example that Iceland topped both GDP per head and internet access.
questions.fix: Say how the two figures tend to move together, quote countries as proof, and flag any country that breaks the pattern.

questions.issue: A number drifted into a different question, such as the pros and cons of education spending.
questions.fix: Keep each point tied to how oil itself could change living standards, for better and for worse.

questions.issue: A number spent time on why more lending may harm the economy, which was not asked.
questions.fix: Stick to the gains: faster growth, lower unemployment, lower inflation and a better current account balance.

questions.topic: Milk price rise and producers' revenue
questions.issue: Most saw the link to soft drinks, but strong analysis of milk producers' revenue needed price elasticity.
questions.fix: Use price elasticity of demand to say whether milk revenue rises or falls.

questions.topic: Economic growth and a current account deficit
questions.issue: A small proportion confused it with a budget deficit, and a higher proportion stayed vague.
questions.fix: Explain why imports or exports would change, for example higher incomes drawing in more imports.

quote.text: A few well developed points will achieve higher marks

takeaways: Learn precise definitions. Reordering the words of the term, or repeating them, earns nothing.
Answer the question that is set. On Paper 11, candidates bent questions on globalisation, company type and packaging to fit what they knew.
Use a new detail from the case for each point, and never write the mirror of a point as your second point.
In part (e) and the (b) questions, make a decision, give a reason for it and say why the other option loses.
When a case question gives data and asks for calculations, show the actual figures, including any loss.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Most candidates understood methods of production in 1(b).
In 2(b), more than 80 per cent got both figures right.
The factors to consider when choosing applicants in 3(c) were generally well answered by most.
Factors affecting the accuracy of market research in 4(a) were well answered.
mistakes: Candidates found 2(a), 2(d) and each part (e) quite challenging, and knowledge of some topics was limited.
Candidates tried to change questions to fit what they knew, most of all in 1(d), 2(d) and 4(e).
Weaker answers confused specialisation with division of labour, and some mixed up a job description with a person specification.
In 3(d), candidates who knew suitable sources of finance often mirrored one point across both, such as interest on a loan and none on retained profit.
Many confused environmentally friendly actions with ethical ones, and the weakest mixed up the product and business cycles.
fix: Give a different application and analysis for each point, because a point only counts once.
Make evaluation a justified decision that grows from your points, not a repeat of them.
Check whether the question wants a reason, an effect or a definition before you answer.
Revise the topics the report names as weak: syllabus sections 1.3.3, 1.4.1, 6.2.1 and 6.3.1.

questions.topic: Advantages to WLT of quality assurance
questions.issue: Some wrote about benefits to customers, and some repeated carpet as the application for both points.
questions.fix: Give benefits to the business, such as fewer complaints and less reworking, each tied to a different case detail.

questions.issue: Some confused globalisation with international trade, and a noticeable number wrote about child labour or quotas.
questions.fix: Explain an opportunity such as new markets and a threat such as more competition, and develop each one.

questions.topic: Improving labour skills to raise productivity
questions.issue: One or two marks was common. Weaker answers repeated the word efficiency or said total output would rise.
questions.fix: Talk about output per worker, and weigh fewer mistakes against the time and cost of training.

questions.issue: A common error was defining a cash flow problem instead of giving reasons for one.
questions.fix: Give causes such as a fall in demand or customers given too long to pay.

questions.issue: Several wrote investors or trade receivables, which are not inflows of money.
questions.fix: Be precise, for example money from investors or payments received from trade receivables.

questions.issue: A common wrong disadvantage was limited funds because it was not a PLC, which answers a different question.
questions.fix: Give an advantage such as limited liability and a disadvantage such as legal formalities.

questions.issue: Not well understood. Very few gave two distinct benefits, and weaker answers said it allows a higher price.
questions.fix: Learn two separate benefits, and make sure the second is not a rewording of the first.

questions.topic: Brand image as a role of packaging
questions.issue: Very few explained how packaging links to brand image, and weaker answers wrote about brand image alone.
questions.fix: Keep packaging at the centre, explain its functions and how it builds the brand, then decide.

papers.title: Short answer and data response
well: Candidates found the paper approachable, and most knew the bulk of the topics well.
The opening (a) and (b) parts went well on the whole, especially 1(a) and 2(b), where most scored.
There were many excellent answers on how a price change affects the break-even chart in 1(c).
Most knew job production and market research methods well.
mistakes: Definitions often lacked precision.
Some were not familiar with why markets become more competitive or with the stages of the business cycle.
Some put analysis in part (c) answers and application in part (e) answers, which are not marked for those skills.
Many part (e) answers had no decision, and most decisions given were not supported.
Mirror arguments, such as interest on a loan against none on equity, only earned credit once.
fix: Know which skills each part rewards. Part (c) gives marks for knowledge, sometimes with application, and part (e) for knowledge, analysis and evaluation only.
Revise the whole syllabus, since a question can come from any area.
Use the stem for application in parts (c) and (d), with a different detail each time.
End part (e) by choosing, saying what tipped the choice, and showing why the other option is weaker.

questions.issue: A common mistake was giving break-even output as a money value instead of units.
questions.fix: Read break-even output on the units axis and break-even revenue on the money axis.

questions.issue: Poorly answered by most. Many assumed full time staff must be more skilled or motivated.
questions.fix: Give benefits that do not depend on such assumptions, and link each to the watch manufacturer.

questions.topic: Job production for a small business
questions.issue: Repetition and mirror points were common, flow production was suggested, and some applied a generic question to FBW.
questions.fix: Develop each point instead of adding new ones, and give a supported decision.

questions.topic: How a business plan reduces risk
questions.issue: Answers such as help decision making were too vague, and some listed parts of a business plan.
questions.fix: Be precise, for example it helps set objectives or supports a request for a loan.

questions.topic: Whether to take on a business partner
questions.issue: Most found development difficult, and a common mistake was discussing who the partner should be.
questions.fix: Focus on whether to have a partner at all, using details such as Gloria being a sole trader.

questions.issue: Most missed the second mark by not saying what an import is. Some confused a tariff with a quota.
questions.fix: Say it is a tax on goods brought into the country from abroad.

questions.topic: Effects of an import quota and currency appreciation
questions.issue: Some confused quotas with tariffs, and many thought appreciation makes imports dearer.
questions.fix: A quota limits the amount imported. Appreciation makes imported materials cheaper.

questions.issue: Most struggled to give a second reason, and different examples of costs only counted once.
questions.fix: Give two separate reasons, not two examples of the same day to day spending.

papers.title: Case study
well: Most came well prepared, and the overall standard was good.
Most appeared to have enough time and answered every question.
Most could give and explain four communication barriers for a large restaurant chain.
Most knew delegation well, and 3(a) on reasons to expand was a strong question.
mistakes: Short and long term finance and economic influences were the least understood topics.
Some barriers to communication were bullet points without enough explanation.
Some found the comparison of two countries quite challenging.
Some weaker answers assumed VP would be the franchisee.
A lack of analysis and evaluation kept answers in the lower levels.
fix: Check how many marks a question carries so you know how far to develop it.
Answer from the point of view of the business, not its employees.
Use a different case example in each section of the (a) questions.
Weigh short term and long term effects to reach the higher levels in a recommendation.

questions.issue: Simple statements about head office keeping control stayed in Level 1.
questions.fix: Develop points such as bulk buying lowering unit costs, and weigh them against storage needs.

questions.issue: Some weaker answers repeated points or wrote generically.
questions.fix: Make four clear points, each tied to the restaurant business, since four marks are for application.

questions.topic: Choosing a country for new restaurants
questions.issue: Some found this quite challenging, and Level 3 needed a justified judgement.
questions.fix: Use the appendix data on costs, wages and unemployment, and say why one country is better and the other worse.

questions.issue: Some listed several reasons briefly instead of developing two.
questions.fix: Develop just two reasons and link each to the restaurant chain.

questions.issue: Not all showed good knowledge of the two methods, and some treated VP as the franchisee.
questions.fix: Remember VP would be the franchisor, receiving fees while the franchisee pays for premises.

questions.topic: Reasons for short and long term finance
questions.issue: Quite a large number seemed unsure of this topic, and some mentioned debts without a reason or a link to VP.
questions.fix: Give a specific reason for each, such as wages in the short term and new equipment in the long term.

questions.issue: Weaker recommendations repeated earlier points.
questions.fix: Use the appendix detail on imported ingredients, and judge which change affects VP the most.

papers.title: Case study
well: As in previous years, the standard was good and very few scripts were weak.
The majority stated at least three characteristics of an entrepreneur.
2(a) on objectives went well, with a large number explaining each objective in context.
The majority answered the leadership styles question well.
mistakes: The least understood topics were incorporated against unincorporated businesses, the aims of a social enterprise, why a cash flow forecast is prepared, and the roles of marketing.
A few explained a characteristic of an entrepreneur by repeating the same word.
Mirror arguments and confusion over limited and unlimited liability held back 1(b).
The majority did not answer 3(a) well, and the most common error was mixing up cash flow with profit.
Weaker answers stayed with simple statements such as saying a change will be more expensive.
fix: Explain a characteristic in new words, saying why it helps an entrepreneur succeed.
Compare the two options the question gives with each other, not with other business types.
When asked for calculations, include the actual profit or loss figure for each option.
Explain why a cost matters, for example higher costs leading to higher prices and lower sales.

questions.issue: The weakest answers gave business factors such as capital or a business plan instead of personal qualities.
questions.fix: Stick to personal qualities, and do not apply a generic question to the case.

questions.topic: Unincorporated business or private limited company
questions.issue: This was challenging, and only the strongest justified the choice and the rejection without repetition.
questions.fix: Explain points such as liability and continuity, and say why the other form loses.

questions.topic: Objectives of ET and a social enterprise
questions.issue: Some said how an objective would be met, not why, and some thought profit is made to pay expenses.
questions.fix: Explain why each body has its objective. Profit is what is left after expenses are paid.

questions.topic: Two options for the first performance
questions.issue: Weaker answers only compared appendix figures, said one option made a loss without the figure, or assumed things the data did not say.
questions.fix: Work out the profit or loss of both options and base your recommendation on those figures.

questions.topic: Why prepare a cash flow forecast
questions.issue: Most who gave reasons did not apply them, and some used words like revenue or finance for inflows and cash.
questions.fix: Give uses such as planning or getting a bank loan, linked to the theatre, and treat it as a forecast.

questions.issue: Weaker answers repeated the question, and a small minority explained how to carry out each role.
questions.fix: Explain why each role matters to the theatre, then justify which is most important.

questions.issue: The most common error confused democratic leadership with delegation, and many answers were generic.
questions.fix: Keep each style under its own heading and link it to managing the theatre staff.

questions.issue: Weaker answers lacked development, and a small number thought fair wages meant equal pay for all.
questions.fix: Weigh the gain against the cost of each change, then say why one affects ET most.

quote.text: It is not possible to hold negative cash

takeaways: Know double entry inside out. Many syllabus topics rest on it, from the suspense account to the provision accounts.
Show your workings for every figure and ratio. A wrong answer with no working earns nothing.
Use proper account names and no abbreviations such as COGS, GP or BBD.
Read the scenario in every advice question closely. Too often, a prepared answer to a different question cost marks.
Practise club accounts as often as business accounts, especially the subscriptions account and what it feeds into.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many candidates had a firm grasp of the basics and got a good share of the questions right.
Questions 1 and 2, on what the accountant provides to managers and on the accounting equation, were answered correctly by most.
Many chose the right statement about depreciation and the right inventory valuation.
mistakes: Some chose a wrong option for how a loss for the year is recorded.
Some found it hard to pick the true statement about a supplier ledger account.
Trade discounts were wrongly picked as a statement of account item by some.
Some valued inventory from the overall totals for cost and net realisable value instead of item by item.
On the limited company question, some chose the option saying dividends must be paid to members.
fix: Read every question slowly before you choose an option.
Work out each type of inventory at whichever is lower, its cost or its net realisable value, and only then add.
Work through the timing of prepaid and accrued amounts with a line for each.
Remember that ordinary shareholders may get no dividend at all if results are poor.

questions.topic: Recording a loss for the year
questions.issue: Some candidates went for a wrong option here.
questions.fix: A loss is credited to the income statement and debited to the capital account.

questions.issue: Some found this challenging and chose a statement that did not fit the account.
questions.fix: A credit balance on the supplier account means the trader owes that supplier money, so it is a liability.

questions.topic: Items on a statement of account
questions.issue: Many were right, but some thought trade discounts would be shown.
questions.fix: Leave trade discount out, since it is taken off before the invoice is recorded.

questions.issue: Some appeared not to notice that option C was about current assets.
questions.fix: Check which kind of asset each option names before you choose.

questions.issue: Some did not carry out the adjustment correctly after repairs were wrongly added to machinery.
questions.fix: Find the depreciation charged on the repairs in error and take it off the provision.

questions.issue: Some found the calculation challenging.
questions.fix: Start with the rent due for the year, then take off the amount prepaid at the start and the amount owing at the end.

questions.issue: Some found this question challenging.
questions.fix: Without opening inventory, cost of sales is understated, which pushes gross profit up.

questions.issue: Plenty got it right, though some struggled.
questions.fix: Cash sales are 10 per cent, so the $36 000 of credit sales is 90 per cent of the total. Find the total first, then apply the net profit margin.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: Many showed sound double entry knowledge and used it on the questions.
Most got the opening questions on what bookkeeping is for and on assets, liabilities and capital right.
Most got the music club concert profit right.
mistakes: Some did not seem to realise that double entry needs both a debit and a credit in the ledger.
Some credited a debt recovered after write off to the irrecoverable receivables account.
Some valued inventory from overall totals instead of item by item.
Many chose a wrong option for the insurance charge, and some put new furniture in the income and expenditure account.
Some miscalculated purchases from the payables figures and found the acid test question challenging.
fix: Check what each question really asks before you pick an option.
Split a charge that spans two rates into its months at each rate.
Keep capital items such as furniture out of the income and expenditure account.
Learn what return and capital employed mean before working out the ratio.

questions.issue: Many were right, but some did not seem to grasp that it needs both a debit and a credit in the ledger.
questions.fix: Double entry means one debit entry and one credit entry in the ledger accounts.

questions.issue: This proved challenging for some, who chose a wrong option.
questions.fix: Decide whether each correction is a debit or a credit in the suspense account, then work back to the starting balance.

questions.issue: The bank debit was usually right, but some put the credit in the irrecoverable receivables account.
questions.fix: Debit bank and credit the debts recovered account.

questions.issue: Some used the overall totals for cost and for net realisable value.
questions.fix: Value each item at the lower of its own cost and net realisable value.

questions.issue: Many picked a wrong answer, though some were right.
questions.fix: Take nine months at the old rate and three months at the new one, then add them.

questions.issue: Many spotted depreciation and subscriptions due, but some included new furniture.
questions.fix: Include income and expenses of the year only. A purchase of furniture is capital spending.

questions.issue: It proved quite hard, yet a significant number still picked the right answer.
questions.fix: Use opening capital plus profit less drawings equals closing capital, and solve for profit.

questions.issue: Some were right, but others did not carry out the calculation correctly.
questions.fix: Take payments to credit suppliers and cash discount, add closing trade payables and take away opening trade payables.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Those who had studied every topic properly reached high grades, and the presentation of most scripts was good.
Many earned high marks on the petty cash book.
The profit or loss on disposal and the retained earnings figure were often worked out correctly.
Many produced good statements of financial position, and many earned full marks on the liquid ratio.
mistakes: In a few scripts, untidy or overwritten figures could not be read.
Many found the provision for doubtful debts account difficult, and many found the motor vehicles accounts challenging.
A large number took the bank balance to be revenue in the manufacturer's income statement.
Many did not see that profit and cash are not the same.
Some discussed a different decision, such as credit or cash trading, when asked whether to stop using cash.
fix: Write clearly, and cross out the attempt you want ignored if you try a question twice.
Put words beside figures, and use full names, not abbreviations.
Show workings for every calculation so some marks can still be earned.
Read the scenario in advice questions carefully and answer the decision actually being made.

questions.issue: Errors included missing the opening balance or the imprest top up, and carrying down the balance before totalling the columns.
questions.fix: Include the opening balance and restoration of the imprest, total the analysis columns, then balance.

questions.issue: A significant number missed that part of the payment came from petty cash, and some added trade discount.
questions.fix: Record each payment from the source it came from, and leave trade discount out.

questions.issue: Common errors were adding trade receivables and moving the whole closing provision to the income statement.
questions.fix: Transfer only the increase in the provision to the income statement.

questions.issue: A common error was taking off one or three years of depreciation instead of two.
questions.fix: Take two years of depreciation off cost to reach the net book value, as the dates in this question required.

questions.issue: Many found this challenging. The report reminds candidates that this account is kept at cost, with no depreciation in it.
questions.fix: Keep the account at cost, and credit the cost of the vehicle sold. Depreciation belongs in its own provision account.

questions.issue: Some did not double the amount where needed, made multiple entries, or used the wrong amount for a difference.
questions.fix: Work out what was done and what should have been done, then post only the difference.

questions.issue: Some left out purchases of finished goods or cost of production, and a large number used the bank balance as revenue.
questions.fix: Use the 50 per cent mark-up on cost of sales to find gross profit and revenue.

questions.topic: Profit but little cash in the bank
questions.issue: Many wrote about expenses, drawings or debenture interest, which do not explain a gap between profit and cash.
questions.fix: Give reasons such as buying non-current assets, repaying loans, paying dividends or building up inventory.

papers.title: Structured questions
well: Standards are still rising, and many candidates were ready for the financial statements questions.
The three column cash book often earned 9 marks or more.
The partnership appropriation account was a strong question, and most scored full marks.
The trading account was straightforward, and three out of four marks was the typical score.
mistakes: Club accounts gave more trouble than other organisations, especially the subscriptions account and how its figure feeds the income and expenditure account.
In the discussion questions, too many wrote a prepared answer that did not fit the question set.
Receipt of capital was entered on both sides of the cash book or called drawings.
In the profit adjustment table, errors three to five were often shown as reducing profit.
In the suspense account, the balance from part (a) was often brought in as balance b/d.
fix: Close off the cash book carefully. A negative cash balance tells you there is an error somewhere.
Balance the cash and bank columns but just total the discount columns.
Name the suspense account entry Trial balance difference, and remember not every error goes through it.
Use net revenue, after returns inwards, in the gross margin, and follow the decimal places asked.

questions.issue: The discount received was regularly left out, and purchase invoices were put on the debit side.
questions.fix: Credit the invoices, and debit the two bank payments with their discount received.

questions.issue: The difference between cash and trade discount was rarely spotted.
questions.fix: Compare the discounts each supplier offers and say how each one lowers the cost of goods.

questions.issue: Errors three to five were often shown as reducing profit, and some put ticks in the table instead of amounts.
questions.fix: Enter the amount or a zero in the right column, and check that the total agrees with the adjusted profit.

questions.issue: Opening balances were often on the wrong side, and the subscriptions written off were frequently left out.
questions.fix: Include the written off subscriptions and transfer the balance to the income and expenditure account.

questions.issue: Many wrote as if the club were a business with customers, ignoring falling membership and rising arrears.
questions.fix: Use the club's own situation on both sides and finish with a clear recommendation.

questions.topic: Receipts and payments account and accumulated fund
questions.issue: Very few gave correct answers, and the accumulated fund was often called capital.
questions.fix: Learn both definitions, including that the fund reflects past surpluses and deficits.

questions.topic: Effect of extra loan interest on a current account
questions.issue: Many found this challenging, and the drop in profit share was completely overlooked.
questions.fix: Add the extra loan interest, then take off the fall in that partner's share of profit.

questions.topic: Changing a partnership into a limited company
questions.issue: Many missed that the two partners would be the only shareholders, so selling shares to others did not apply.
questions.fix: Build every point around who would own the shares in this case.

quote.text: Candidates should not be afraid of coming to a judgement.

takeaways: Read each question carefully before writing. Several were misread, such as employee duties to a business being taken as the business's duties to employees.
Half the marks on a 12 mark question are for evaluation, so give it a fair share of your answer and finish with a definite, justified decision.
Apply to the named business with real detail from its industry. Repeating its name or copying the case is not application.
Give exactly what the question asks for: one weakness, two benefits, or one advantage and one disadvantage. Extra points earn nothing.
On Paper 4, stay on the topic the question names and use only the data that matters most. Copying the timeline wastes time.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Answers on one way to cut variable costs were more confident than the fixed cost definitions.
Most could define product differentiation accurately and in full.
Most understood product development and gave a clear reason why it matters to a business.
Most defined commission well, and most explained one type of training with confidence.
Most who chose the inventory question gave sound answers, and many handled the SMART objectives question well.
mistakes: Many gave only part of a definition of fixed costs, such as costs that do not change.
Some offered several ways to cut variable costs, so they did not develop the single way the question wanted.
Weaker answers mixed up product development and product differentiation.
A significant number misread Question 4 and wrote about the business's responsibilities to employees.
Many struggled with what supply chain management means, and many stopped at analysis without reaching a judgement.
Weaker ethics answers tended to treat it as a plain HRM question and said little about moral issues in mining.
fix: Check who owes what to whom in any stakeholder question before you start.
Take each benefit through knowledge, application and analysis in turn, so you do not drift into side topics.
Put detailed context into your concluding evaluation, such as electric car manufacturing or mining, not only into the analysis.
Answer the exact claim in the question, such as whether ethics should always shape HRM in mining.

questions.issue: Many wrote only that the costs do not change. Some confused costs with prices.
questions.fix: Say fixed costs stay the same when the level of output changes.

questions.issue: Some gave several ways and did not develop and apply the one asked for.
questions.fix: Give one way, such as switching to a cheaper raw material supplier or bulk buying, and develop it.

questions.issue: Less successful answers used it to mean the range of products in a firm's portfolio.
questions.fix: Say it is making a product distinctive from rivals, often with a unique feature.

questions.issue: A significant number wrote about what the business owes employees, not the reverse.
questions.fix: Analyse one duty employees have, such as keeping to their contract or working productively, and its effect on the business.

questions.issue: It was not a popular choice, but most who chose it gave sound answers. The risk was drifting into JIT or the drawbacks.
questions.fix: Use benefits such as meeting sudden demand or keeping production going if supplies are disrupted.

questions.topic: Supply chain management for an electric car manufacturer
questions.issue: Many did not judge whether it is the most important activity, and evaluation was often general.
questions.fix: Use car specific parts such as batteries, then judge its importance against other operational activities for this maker.

questions.issue: Some misread the question or had enough material for only one reason.
questions.fix: Pick two of the five SMART letters and build one analysed reason from each.

questions.topic: Ethics and HRM in a mining business
questions.issue: Many weakened their evaluation by not linking it to the features of mining.
questions.fix: Use mining issues like health and safety, weigh caring HRM against its cost, and respond to the word always.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Explaining a factor that influences supply was handled more confidently.
Most could define equality clearly, linking it to fair treatment of all employees.
The USP benefits question was a popular choice, and most handled it well.
Better answers on stakeholder conflict focused on its effects, such as demotivated workers, slow decisions or industrial action.
mistakes: Many gave only part of a definition of demand.
Many could not identify one stage of the transformational process. Some focused on added value or covered several stages.
Some were unsure what diversity means, so the benefit they gave was vague.
Many described types of stakeholder and how conflict starts, instead of how conflict affects the business.
Many had little understanding of working capital and drifted into management styles.
Many turned the coffee shop essay into an essay on the marketing mix.
fix: Spend your effort on the effect asked for, not on describing the background.
When a question asks whether one factor is most important, compare it with other factors before judging.
Put explicit features of the named business into your judgement, such as a small retailer or a new coffee shop.
Analyse two benefits when two are asked for.

questions.issue: Many wrote only the quantity customers want to buy.
questions.fix: Add willing and able, at a given price, over a period of time.

questions.issue: Many did not identify a stage. Some focused on added value or referred to several stages.
questions.fix: Name one stage, such as input or output, and explain only that stage.

questions.issue: Some did not understand diversity, so their answers were vague.
questions.fix: Define diversity as a range of skills, experiences and characteristics, then explain one benefit such as more creativity.

questions.topic: Effect of stakeholder conflict on a business
questions.issue: Many explained different stakeholders and how conflict might occur in great detail, missing the effect on the business.
questions.fix: Pick one effect, such as industrial action cutting production, and chain it through to customers and survival.

questions.topic: Benefits of government grants as finance
questions.issue: Less successful answers explained why grants are given. Some analysed only one benefit.
questions.fix: Use benefits such as no interest or repayment, and not giving up equity or control.

questions.topic: Poor working capital management and small retailer failure
questions.issue: Many had little understanding of working capital. A significant number never evaluated, and many judgements were very general.
questions.fix: Compare it with other causes of failure, then judge using features of a small retailer, such as paying suppliers.

questions.topic: Benefits of a product with a USP
