questions.issue: Well answered by most, but some analysed only one benefit.
questions.fix: Analyse two benefits, such as charging a premium price and building brand loyalty.

questions.topic: Marketing and the success of a new coffee shop
questions.issue: Weaker answers wrote long accounts of the 4Ps and advertising instead of weighing other success factors.
questions.fix: Compare marketing with other factors a coffee shop needs, then judge using coffee shop details.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Overall, knowledge of the syllabus was good across both sections of the paper.
Most earned at least one mark for defining social enterprise, and most earned both marks for dismissal.
Answers on weaknesses of family businesses were often developed for two or three marks.
Many scored 5 marks or more on the external recruitment question, which was the most popular choice.
The low price airline essay was well answered overall, with most showing knowledge, application and analysis.
mistakes: Weaker answers on social enterprise mentioned only the triple bottom line.
Most found it hard to explain how the business meets the human need they had named.
Less successful answers confused the mass market with mass marketing.
Many assumed more output guarantees more sales and profit, and some confused labour productivity with labour intensive.
The belief that a cash flow forecast shows profit still appeared.
Very few applied break-even analysis to a bicycle maker, and evaluation was often very limited or missing.
fix: For explain questions, write two or three developed sentences, not a single line or a page.
Use linking phrases like because, therefore and as a result to develop each point.
Label your points, for example the first purpose is, then the second purpose is.
Use the industry's own words for context, such as frames and chains or cabin crew and tickets, not just the business type.
Make a critical judgement instead of repeating what you have already said.

questions.issue: Weaker answers referred only to the triple bottom line, which earned one mark.
questions.fix: Mention social objectives and reinvesting profits to benefit society.

questions.topic: Satisfying a human need at work
questions.issue: Many named a need but could not explain how the business satisfies it.
questions.fix: Pick one need, such as social needs, and show how something like teamwork meets it.

questions.issue: Many said it is aimed at the whole market but left out the marketing part, such as targeting or selling.
questions.fix: Say it means selling to, or targeting, the whole market or most of it.

questions.issue: Definitions earned nothing here. Many assumed more output means more sales and profit, and analysis was generally limited.
questions.fix: Give a reason, such as meeting large orders, then develop it, for example into customer trust and loyalty.

questions.topic: Purposes of a cash flow forecast
questions.issue: The majority focused on getting a bank loan or paying bills. Few covered other purposes such as monitoring debtors.
questions.fix: Give two distinct purposes and develop each, for example spotting a wage payment gap and arranging an overdraft.

questions.topic: Break-even analysis for a new bicycle manufacturer
questions.issue: Most showed limited knowledge of break-even analysis, and very few used the bicycle context.
questions.fix: Learn its main advantages and disadvantages, then judge it against other finance activities such as cash flow.

questions.issue: Some wrote about recruitment agencies. Responses quite often gave three or more advantages.
questions.fix: Analyse two benefits, such as new ideas leading to an innovative product, and develop each one.

questions.topic: Motivated workforce and a low price airline
questions.issue: Supported judgements in context were in the minority. Less successful answers made very basic conclusions.
questions.fix: Weigh motivated staff against what low price passengers care about, such as cheap fares or marketing, and judge in airline context.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Naming one barrier to entrepreneurship was very well done.
The vast majority who knew how to work out market share by revenue scored full marks.
Question 2 went well overall, and knowledge of its main topics was strong.
Most handled the question on ways to motivate young people to work on the farms well.
mistakes: In the part (a) questions, many used case examples or copied case text, which earned nothing.
Many explained a partnership without saying it is a form of ownership.
Demand was given as a factor influencing supply, and it was not accepted.
A significant majority seemed unsure what an overdraft is, and most wrote about loans instead.
A significant majority gave the 2022 labour productivity figure instead of the expected 2023 figure.
Some analysed the factory decision well but never gave a judgement, losing the 6 evaluation marks.
fix: Answer part (a) from your own knowledge, not the case.
Keep 3 mark answers short so you have time for the 8 and 12 mark questions.
Give each knowledge point its own piece of case application.
Put a definite judgement at the end, after the analysis. Saying both are important is not specific enough.

questions.issue: Many described running or managing a business rather than owning it.
questions.fix: Say it is a form of business ownership, then add a feature such as unlimited liability.

questions.topic: Factor influencing the supply of GR's products
questions.issue: Demand was not accepted. Two pieces of case detail were needed for application.
questions.fix: Choose a supply factor such as costs of production, and use two specific facts about GR.

questions.topic: Advantage and disadvantage of a bank overdraft
questions.issue: Most described loans, and some even said overdrafts suit long term use. Points like paying interest apply to all borrowing.
questions.fix: Define it as a short term facility to withdraw more than the account balance, then give points specific to overdrafts.

questions.topic: Price or promotion as the most important element
questions.issue: Half the marks were for evaluation, and many opened with a one line judgement.
questions.fix: Write one paragraph on price, one on promotion, then a final paragraph judging which matters more for GR.

questions.topic: Element of the triple bottom line
questions.issue: Generally well answered, but workers, customers and factors of production were not accepted.
questions.fix: Name one of the three elements using the correct term.

questions.issue: Challenging for many. The difference between selling price and the cost of raw materials was seldom seen.
questions.fix: Say added value is the difference between the selling price and the cost of the raw materials bought in.

questions.issue: A significant majority gave the 2022 figure. Without working, that scored nothing.
questions.fix: Raise the output by the expected growth first, then divide by the number of farmers, and show your working.

questions.topic: Motivating young people to work on the farms
questions.issue: A number gave increased motivation as the outcome, which only repeats the question.
questions.fix: Give two methods, each with its own case detail, and take each to an outcome such as higher productivity.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: The vast majority could name a quality an entrepreneur needs, such as determination.
Opportunity cost was understood well on the whole, and many gave a textbook definition.
Most could apply the market share formula, and the term was fairly well known.
On the electric scooter question, most kept to one advantage and one disadvantage as asked.
Both cases were accessible, and most finished the paper.
mistakes: Many exemplified the choice in opportunity cost but not the benefit given up.
In the closing balance, the commonest mistakes were missing the negative sign and leaving out the opening balance.
Many gave generic factors for choosing finance, and some recommended a source of finance instead.
Long definitions of induction training used up time without earning extra marks.
Many answers on accurate cost information had little or no evaluation.
In the marketing mix question it was common to change every one of the 4Ps, leaving little time to evaluate.
fix: Write one or two words for identify questions.
Do not spend long on definitions when most marks are for application.
Build each analysis point into a developed chain that ends with an effect on the business.
Give evaluation about half of a 12 mark answer, and judge in the context of the business.

questions.issue: Candidates often showed the choice being made but not the lost benefit.
questions.fix: Explain both parts: the choice between options and the benefit of the option given up.

questions.issue: The two most common mistakes were not seeing the answer is negative and leaving out the opening balance.
questions.fix: Add each month's net cash flow to its opening balance, carry the closing balance forward as the next opening balance, keep the signs, and show your working.

questions.topic: Factor influencing the choice of a source of finance
questions.issue: Some recommended a source of finance, and many gave generic answers limited to 1 mark.
questions.fix: Explain one factor, such as how long the money is needed, using facts about Markus and OFD.

questions.issue: The most common format was a brief conclusion that repeated the earlier arguments.
questions.fix: Argue both sides, evaluate each point, then reach an overall judgement about OFD.

questions.issue: Some gave environmental answers, which is the A Level meaning, and these were often vague.
questions.fix: Use the AS meaning: being able to keep production at its current level in the future.

questions.topic: Market share of the mountain bike market
questions.issue: Errors came from adding up the market size wrongly, leaving out MXB's sales, or inverting the formula.
questions.fix: Include MXB in the total market, then divide its sales by the total and multiply by 100.

questions.topic: Reason why MXB's objectives may change
questions.issue: Only answers applied to MXB could earn the application marks.
questions.fix: Use the case numbers, such as the fall in MXB's sales, to support your reason.

questions.topic: Changing the marketing mix to extend the product life cycle
questions.issue: Many tried to do too much, building a whole new mix instead of changes to the existing one.
questions.fix: Choose one or two changes, analyse them, then judge how likely they are to extend the life cycle.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Most could name one of the 4Ps when asked for an element of the marketing mix.
Most identified the correct data and completed the labour turnover calculation.
Nearly all named a sensible way to cut labour turnover, such as a pay rise.
Many showed clear working on the closing balance calculation, and the question went well.
On Steve's management style, answers were strong and used the case well.
mistakes: Some explained consumer market by repeating its own words.
Most could name two costs of going international, yet they did not always analyse the effect or link it to FM.
Some confused stakeholders with shareholders.
Many said stock arrives just in time without explaining what that means.
When the closing balance was wrong, the slip was often in net cash flow, usually from taking inflows away from outflows.
Very few applied the disadvantage of a co-operative to the case.
fix: Keep identify answers short and do not define the wider topic.
Write two separate paragraphs for the two points in part (c), each with its own context.
Start part (d) with brief definitions of at least two of the terms in the question.
Make sure every suggestion is realistic for the business in the case.

questions.issue: Some said it is the market for consumers, which explains nothing.
questions.fix: Say consumers are the final users, selling business to consumer rather than to other businesses.

questions.issue: Some inverted the equation, though showing the steps could still earn marks.
questions.fix: Divide the number of employees who left by the total number of employees and multiply by 100.

questions.topic: Impacts on costs of entering international markets
questions.issue: Two costs were usually named, but the impact was not always developed and FM's details were not always used.
questions.fix: Name a cost, say whether it will rise or fall, and analyse the effect on FM.

questions.topic: Impact on stakeholders of a change from batch production to mass customisation
questions.issue: Some confused stakeholder with shareholder. The last mark needed an overall judgement in context.
questions.fix: Define two of the terms, then judge which stakeholder is most likely to be affected.

questions.issue: Many did not explain the phrase. Some thought it is about delivering goods to customers.
questions.fix: Say it is inventory management that keeps stock at or near zero, with materials arriving as production needs them.

questions.issue: Errors were often in net cash flow, done by taking inflows from outflows. Some used numbers with no clear source.
questions.fix: Net cash flow is inflows minus outflows. Add it to the opening balance, and show where every figure comes from.

questions.topic: Disadvantage to employees of being a co-operative
questions.issue: Very few used the case. Some seemed to think owners and employees are different people here.
questions.fix: Remember the employees are the owners, then use case detail about GD.

questions.topic: Sources of finance for the new shop
questions.issue: Context was at times limited, and some suggestions, such as crowdfunding $2 million quickly, were unrealistic.
questions.fix: Choose realistic sources, such as a bank loan or mortgage, and explain what each means for opening the shop.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: Questions 1 and 2 went well, and many answers earned 7 or 8 marks with developed chains in context.
Many recognised that Questions 1 and 2 need no evaluation.
Most worked out the seasonal variation correctly using the right formula.
Many applied the correct equation for forecast revenue.
The economic policy question appeared to be the most accessible 12 mark question.
mistakes: Many did not have the core knowledge of business concepts that good answers are built on.
A common error in Question 1 was analysing more than two benefits or adding evaluation.
Some confused quality assurance with quality control.
Most did not know the ROCE equation, and few included all three parts of capital employed.
Many debated whether WP should invest instead of whether the information was sufficient.
In the 12 mark questions, many gave little real evaluation.
fix: Look through every question before you read the case, so you read it with a purpose.
Interpret case data. Repeating it does not earn application marks.
Keep analysis short in 12 mark questions, since one developed chain earns both analysis marks.
Spend about half of each 12 mark answer on evaluation.

questions.issue: A common error was analysing more than two benefits or adding evaluation. Some confused it with quality control.
questions.fix: Analyse two benefits, such as less waste of wood leading to better margins, in context.

questions.issue: Some wrote about external communication. Many developed only one limitation in context.
questions.fix: Develop two limitations in context, such as one-way communication giving the 35 employees little say.

questions.issue: The majority got this right. The answer had to be shown as a negative figure.
questions.fix: Subtract the trend value from the revenue for that quarter and keep the minus sign.

questions.topic: Sales forecasts from time series analysis in business planning
questions.issue: Many wrote far more analysis than needed and showed knowledge of forecasting but not of planning.
questions.fix: Link the forecast to planning resources such as skilled labour, then evaluate its reliability in WP's context.

questions.issue: Few added all three parts of capital employed, and most could not recall the ROCE equation, which scored nothing.
questions.fix: Add issued share capital, reserves and non-current liabilities for capital employed, then divide profit from operations by it and multiply by 100. Set the working out clearly.

questions.topic: Whether the financial information is sufficient
questions.issue: This proved the most difficult extended question. Many judged the investment rather than the information.
questions.fix: Use the ROCE, gearing and profit data, then say what other information, such as investment appraisal, is missing.

questions.topic: Effects of the new economic policy measures
questions.issue: Evaluation was often limited to saying a private limited company would not be affected.
questions.fix: Consider indirect effects, such as lower disposable income reducing demand for toys, and how uncertain the timing is.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: Many scripts were excellent, well structured and focused on the questions.
Many reached 7 or 8 marks on the two analyse questions, Questions 1 and 2.
Question 2 was the most accessible, and the majority spotted two-way communication.
Most could work out the current ratio correctly.
Most understood what sustainability means for a business.
mistakes: Some only explained OV's current marketing strategy, often by copying the case.
Many current ratio answers were not written as a ratio.
Errors were frequent in working out capital employed for ROCE.
Some said becoming a plc means government control, which scored zero.
Many did not calculate average investment for ARR.
Many repeated the location table at length without saying why factors mattered.
fix: Define key terms to secure knowledge marks.
Analyse only two impacts or benefits in Questions 1 and 2, with no evaluation.
Use your calculation results as evidence in the evaluate questions that follow.
Focus on two or three key factors and judge which matters most.

questions.topic: Marketing strategy changes to sell to retailers
questions.issue: Some only described the current strategy by copying the case.
questions.fix: Show what must change for business buyers, such as a lower price so retailers can make a profit.

questions.topic: Benefits of OV's methods of communicating with employees
questions.issue: Many developed only one benefit in context. A few wrote about training or leadership instead.
questions.fix: Link two-way communication to motivation, then to productivity and profit, for both benefits.

questions.issue: There were no method marks, and many did not express the answer as a ratio.
questions.fix: Divide current assets by current liabilities and write the answer as a ratio.

questions.issue: Capital employed was often worked out wrongly.
questions.fix: Divide profit from operations by capital employed and multiply by 100. Show full working so you can still earn the own figure mark.

questions.topic: Whether shareholders benefit from becoming a plc
questions.issue: Evaluation often recommended whether OV should become a plc, missing the focus on shareholders.
questions.fix: Weigh gains such as higher dividends or share price against losses such as separation of ownership and control.

questions.issue: Many skipped the average investment step and so got 20 per cent.
questions.fix: Use average profit divided by average investment, multiplied by 100, and give a percentage.

questions.issue: Many repeated the data without saying why factors were relevant.
questions.fix: Pick two or three factors and link them to the case, for example a lower capital cost when gearing is already high.

questions.topic: Impact of the growing importance of sustainability
questions.issue: Many balanced answers lacked evaluative development and gave only chains of analysis.
questions.fix: Judge how serious the threat is to OV, or compare sustainability with price and taste for customers.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: The case was very accessible, and most understood how online tour booking works.
Many handled the barriers to communication question well.
Many gave quite good answers on how LT could check whether tours meet expectations.
Nearly all calculated the payback period correctly, and many calculated price elasticity correctly with the negative sign.
Most knew what an employment contract is and how it differs from LT's casual arrangement with guides.
mistakes: Many used the old ARR formula, or made one slip such as not deducting the investment or not dividing by the number of years.
Some answers were generic textbook knowledge with little use of the case.
Some misread the negative signs in elasticity and judged both tours elastic or both inelastic.
fix: Learn the published syllabus formulae, as some differ from older versions.
Spend 10 to 15 minutes reading the case, and use the line references.
Write two developed points in two paragraphs for the 8 mark questions.
Consider other views, such as whether the new venture moves LT away from its original business model.

questions.topic: Barriers to communication from online operations
questions.issue: The best answers split the two barriers into two paragraphs.
questions.fix: Use barriers like misunderstood tour needs or time differences, and chain them to customers switching and lost sales.

questions.issue: The best answers used two separate paragraphs, one for each way.
questions.fix: Suggest after tour questionnaires or interviews, then show how LT would use the feedback.

questions.issue: Many used the old formula, or forgot to deduct the investment or divide by the number of years.
questions.fix: Average profit is total net cash flow minus the investment, divided by the years. Divide it by average investment and multiply by 100. Stating the formula can earn a mark.

questions.topic: Investing in the new Tour Hub
questions.issue: Most used their calculations positively, and many also saw the risks, such as reliance on the cruise company.
questions.fix: Weigh payback and ARR against the risks, and question how reliable the forecasts are.

questions.issue: Many got it right with the negative sign. Others gained part marks for the percentage changes or the formula.
questions.fix: Divide the percentage change in quantity demanded by the percentage change in price and keep the negative sign.

questions.topic: Whether PED is sufficient for pricing decisions
questions.issue: Some confused the negative signs and judged both tours the same.
questions.fix: Compare the inelastic shopping tours with the elastic street food tours, then add factors like costs and competitors.

questions.topic: Employment contracts with guaranteed tours for some guides
questions.issue: Good answers balanced both sides. The risks included demotivating guides not chosen and paying for tours in low season.
questions.fix: Weigh reliable service from popular guides against higher costs and loyalty problems, then conclude for LT.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Many knew a broad range of business concepts and could use them.
More than half achieved 7 or 8 analysis marks on the takeover question.
Most reached at least a basic verdict on whether taking over PS was the right call.
Most completed both questions in the time.
mistakes: Some only listed what SWOT stands for without showing they understood it.
Only a few added what their verdict depended on or a second line of evaluation, so few reached full evaluation marks.
Some copied the case word for word.
On the operations question, some discussed marketing, HRM or other departments.
Some used strategic analysis tools such as PEST or core competencies instead of operations strategies.
High evaluation marks on the operations question were limited to a small number.
fix: Define terms inside your explanation, for example what a lower trade receivables turnover means.
Counter each point straight after you analyse it, with its own chain.
Analyse two operations strategies, then recommend one and explain why it suits the business.
After your judgement, add what it depends on, in context.

questions.topic: Whether taking over PS was the correct strategic decision
questions.issue: Strong answers that fell short of full marks were usually one Level 3 analysis point and one Level 3 evaluation point short.
questions.fix: Make two balanced chains on issues like inventory control or finances, and say what your judgement depends on.

questions.topic: Operations strategy to overcome LH's problems
questions.issue: Some fixed on the IT and quality problems or other departments instead of operations strategies.
questions.fix: Use strategies such as quality assurance, JIT, lean production or automation, weigh a drawback such as cost, then recommend one.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Some argued very well that BV's decisions, a key function of leadership, led to its effective strategic management.
The best candidates combined several examples from the data into one chain to reach a judgement.
mistakes: Many had clearly revised for questions other than the two that came up.
On the country X question, it was not unusual to find answers with no marketing in them.
Some analysed BV's strategic management without linking it to any leadership function.
Among the most common faults was rewriting the timeline and appendices, sometimes whole appendices.
Many treated the advise question as a chance to write about SWOT, PEST and other strategic tools.
Some spent too long on one question and left only an outline for the other.
fix: Revise the whole syllabus, not only the strategy topics.
Aim for 25 to 30 minutes per question with three or four developed chains.
Be selective with data. Leaving some out is fine.
Make a clear decision that follows from your arguments, then weigh what could change it.

questions.topic: Leadership and BV's effective strategic management
questions.issue: Some analysed strategic management with no link to leadership, so large parts were irrelevant.
questions.fix: Use leadership functions such as decision-making, communication and motivation, and combine several examples into one judgement.

questions.topic: Marketing strategy for entering country X
questions.issue: Most often, answers analysed the tools as the subject instead of giving advice on marketing.
questions.fix: Advise on a strategy, for example a pan-global approach against keeping local differences, and give a clear recommendation.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: The stronger answers picked a marketing activity, showed how RHR used it, then set its strengths against its weaknesses.
On the core competence question, stronger answers took the three competencies in the case and tested each against the new city hotels.
mistakes: Weaker answers retold the case and added no analysis.
Some discussed things that were not marketing, such as becoming a Ltd, HR and training, or financing growth.
Some suggested alternative or future marketing instead of judging what had already happened.
Some used SWOT, Ansoff, PESTLE or tools like blue ocean in the marketing question.
Weaker core competence answers listed and defined every strategic approach, at times with no link to RHR.
Many did not finish the second question because they spent too long on the first.
fix: Plan your time: about 15 minutes reading and planning, then about 30 minutes per essay.
Choose two or three marketing activities and judge each both ways.
Analyse the approach the question names, then contrast it with one or two others.
State clearly whether the approach is enough, and support your answer with RHR's context.

questions.issue: Some wrote about other functions, future plans or strategic tools instead of judging past marketing.
questions.fix: Take activities such as the pan-global approach, weigh economies of scale against ignoring local culture, then judge.

questions.topic: Whether a core competence framework is sufficient
questions.issue: Some evaluated opening the city hotels instead of the approach. Some thought the city hotels were already open.
questions.fix: Analyse the three competencies, compare with one or two approaches such as SWOT, then judge whether the framework is enough.

quote.text: Examiners are not looking for the one correct answer

takeaways: A judgement has to answer the question set. A summary of your earlier points is not evaluation, and the best judgements use the context of the business named.
When a question asks for one way or two impacts, give exactly that number. Extra points earn nothing and take time away from developing the ones that count.
Use the case as evidence, especially its numbers. Copying it out, or ignoring it, both cost you application marks.
Learn the syllabus formulae and show every step of working, with the right unit, so you can still collect method marks.
Explain a term in different words from the term itself, and learn the less familiar ones such as trade credit, curriculum vitae and blue ocean strategy.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Most candidates gave a clear definition of labour turnover, and most defined capital intensive well.
The benefit of labour intensive operations was well answered by most, and every candidate knew what those operations are.
Most explained a way to lower the break-even level of output well.
Most knew what a dynamic business environment is, and many built well reasoned chains on how it affects a business.
On mass marketing, candidates knew marketing well and could explain how it lifts sales.
mistakes: Several candidates mixed up a workforce plan with organisational structure or a plan of someone's working day, which scored nothing.
Some gave only half a definition of margin of safety, or confused it with health and safety, buffer stock or break-even point itself.
A minority got the direction wrong on break-even, for example suggesting higher costs or a price cut.
Some confused a dynamic business environment with diversity, delegation or motivation.
Some confused mass marketing with mass production or niche marketing, and some spent time on its drawbacks when only advantages were asked for.
Many essay conclusions only summarised earlier points instead of giving a judgement.
fix: Keep each definition to one or two sentences. For labour turnover, give the rate and the idea of employees leaving.
When the question asks for one role or one way, write about just one. Extra ones gain no marks.
Do not open an 8 mark answer with a definition the question does not ask for. Go straight to the advantages or ways.
Save evaluation for the 12 mark parts. The 8 mark parts test analysis only.
In 12 mark essays, make a developed judgement and keep it in the context given, such as the primary sector or a software firm.

questions.issue: Several confused it with organisational structure, task allocation or a daily work plan. Most earned two marks for a basic explanation that was not developed.
questions.fix: Say the plan works out how many staff the business will need for its future objectives, then add why that helps.

questions.issue: Some said only that a lot of machinery is used. Answers that treated capital as finance scored nothing.
questions.fix: Compare the amount of machinery with the amount of labour used.

questions.issue: Some wrote only above break-even point, and some confused it with marginal costs or safety needs.
questions.fix: Refer to both current output and break-even output. A correctly labelled break-even chart also earns the marks.

questions.topic: Effect of a dynamic business environment
questions.issue: A definition alone earned nothing. Some wrote about diversity, internal management or HR issues instead.
questions.fix: Pick one change, such as new competitors entering, and follow its effect on one area of the business, such as marketing.

questions.topic: Product differentiation in primary sector businesses
questions.issue: Some confused differentiation with diversification. Some only agreed with the question instead of judging it.
questions.fix: Weigh the benefits against limits such as cost or rivals copying, then give a developed judgement that refers to the primary sector.

questions.issue: Some wrote about the effect on employees only, often motivation, without linking it back to the business. Some ways overlapped.
questions.fix: Give two clearly separate ways and show how each helps the business run better.

questions.topic: McClelland's three needs theory in a software business
questions.issue: Many wrote about Maslow, Herzberg, Taylor or Mayo and showed no knowledge of McClelland. Applying it to a software firm was hard for many.
questions.fix: Analyse at least two of McClelland's needs against the kinds of workers a software business employs, then judge which matters most.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Most scored two marks or more on the advantage of a person specification to an employer.
Most gave clear definitions of business enterprise.
Many took all three marks for a reason why a business might fail.
Many knew retained earnings well and earned all three marks for an advantage of using them.
Many handled the new airline essay well, using airline details such as flights, tickets and destinations to good effect.
mistakes: A significant number confused job description with person specification and wrote about the skills of applicants.
Weaker answers on person specification gave advantages to the applicant instead of the employer.
Very few candidates showed that bankruptcy is a legal process, not just a business running out of money.
On self-actualisation, many described lower levels of Maslow without showing how meeting them leads to self-actualisation.
On linking marketing and corporate objectives, most could name objectives of each kind but generally left the connection between the two sets unexplained.
Many essay conclusions were only a summary of earlier points.
fix: For job description, write about the tasks, duties and responsibilities of the job, not the qualities of the person.
Check who the advantage is for before you write. The person specification question asked about employers.
On Question 4 style questions, marks start only when you name a way to improve efficiency, so name it early.
Finish every 12 mark essay with a concluding judgement in context, even if you used the context earlier.

questions.issue: A significant number wrote about what applicants should be like, which belongs in a person specification.
questions.fix: Define it through the tasks, duties and responsibilities of a particular job.

questions.issue: Weaker answers stopped at the business running out of money. Hardly anyone mentioned the legal side.
questions.fix: Say it is a legal procedure when a business cannot repay what it owes.

questions.issue: Explaining what efficiency means scored nothing by itself. The first mark came only from naming a way to improve it.
questions.fix: Name one way, such as new technology, staff training or motivation, then apply and analyse it.

questions.issue: Many stayed on the lower levels of Maslow. Even stronger answers did not analyse well how the measures led to self-actualisation.
questions.fix: Use methods such as job enrichment, a say in decisions or promotion, and show step by step how each leads to self-actualisation.

questions.topic: Motivating others as a hotel manager's role
questions.issue: Better answers compared motivating with other roles, but high evaluation marks needed the final section to be clearly about a hotel.
questions.fix: Compare motivating staff with roles such as setting objectives or managing finance, then judge using hotel details like guests, chefs and receptionists.

questions.topic: Link between marketing and corporate objectives
questions.issue: Most who chose it struggled. Many named relevant objectives but gave no analysis of how aligning them helps the business.
questions.fix: Take one corporate objective, such as market share, and show how marketing objectives that support it benefit the business.

questions.topic: Lowest prices and a new airline's success
questions.issue: The concluding section had to judge the view in clear airline context to earn high evaluation marks.
questions.fix: Weigh low prices against safety, quality and competition in the low price market, and end with a judgement about airlines specifically.

papers.title: Business concepts 1
well: Most candidates handled the organic growth definition comfortably.
Many gained full marks for defining venture capital.
On the whole the intrapreneur question went well, with qualities such as creativity and risk taking often described and put in context.
Evaluation in the 5(b) and 6(b) essays is improving, with more candidates attempting it.
mistakes: Curriculum vitae was an unknown term for a significant number of candidates.
Many did not really know what trade credit is.
Many named a reason to stay small but did not apply or explain it.
Some described the benefit of an employment contract to the employer when the question asked about the employee.
Some answers to the 8 mark questions covered just one factor, and the analysis was often thin.
Many essays lacked a strong concluding judgement in context.
fix: Learn every syllabus term, including documents like a CV and short term finance like trade credit.
In the 8 mark questions, give exactly two factors and push the analysis further, not just the application.
End each essay with a section that responds directly to the view in the question.
Describe the features of the business in that conclusion, such as a retail clothing business or a hospital, even if you did so earlier.

questions.topic: Reason a business may choose to remain small
questions.issue: Many named a reason such as lack of finance or fear of losing control, but did not explain why the owner would prefer that.
questions.fix: Give one reason and explain it, for example avoiding the higher risks and extra staff that growth brings.

questions.issue: A significant number did not know the term at all.
questions.fix: Say it is a document listing a person's education, qualifications and past work experience.

questions.issue: Weaker answers repeated the words of the term. Some confused it with a joint venture.
questions.fix: Say it is risk capital invested in a business by venture capitalists.

questions.issue: Many found this hard, as many showed little real grasp of what trade credit is.
questions.fix: Explain it as buying from suppliers now and paying later, then give one drawback such as losing early payment discounts or late fees.

questions.topic: Product portfolio analysis and marketing decisions
questions.issue: Weaker answers lacked knowledge of product portfolio analysis.
questions.fix: Show how seeing the strengths and weaknesses of all products guides one decision, such as replacing a weak product, and link it to the product life cycle.

questions.topic: Ethics and the marketing of retail clothing businesses
questions.issue: Weaker answers did not understand ethical business activity. Many gave weak concluding judgements.
questions.fix: Use examples from both making and selling clothes, then respond directly to the view with clear retail clothing detail.

questions.topic: Supply chain management in a hospital
questions.issue: Weaker answers understood supply chain management only partly and struggled to relate it to a hospital.
questions.fix: Remember hospitals rely on equipment and supplies too, then judge the impact with detailed hospital context in your conclusion.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Naming a motivator that is not financial went well for most.
Piece rate was understood by most, and many took two or more of its three marks.
Many earned full marks on the marketing mix question, applying the two elements well to the case.
Some candidates scored full marks on the payment method and employee development question.
Business objectives were well known, and candidates could give two reasons why DN might change them.
mistakes: Most did not work out the change between profit before and after the new product.
A few gave a financial motivator, such as fringe benefits.
Many listed all four elements of the marketing mix before picking two.
Some described two objectives instead of giving reasons why they would change.
Some were unsure about supply chain management and wrote about raw materials or delivering printed magazines, though the business provides online content.
fix: Read the calculation question carefully and show your workings every time.
Answer part (a) from knowledge only. It does not need the case.
Write about only as many elements as the question asks for.
In both part (d) answers, give a balanced argument and a justified recommendation without repeating earlier points.
Use the case information inside your answer instead of copying it.

questions.issue: Many scored only one mark for working out a revenue, cost or profit figure. Most did not find the difference.
questions.fix: Work out profit without the new product and profit with it, then subtract one from the other.

questions.topic: Using cost information to improve performance
questions.issue: Weaker answers described types of cost or ways to raise revenue.
questions.fix: Name a use of cost information, such as setting prices or forecasting profit, and link it to PS's performance.

questions.topic: Marketing mix for the new packaging
questions.issue: Many stated all four elements first, though only two were needed.
questions.fix: Pick two elements straight away and analyse each in context.

questions.issue: Most stopped at 2 marks, with no development or example to earn the third.
questions.fix: Explain the meaning, then add an example of a secondary source to secure the last mark.

questions.issue: A few used the wrong pair of years.
questions.fix: Check the years in the question, then divide the change by the original figure and multiply by 100.

questions.issue: Some described research methods. Most named useful data but did not explain why it would help DN.
questions.fix: Name one piece of data, such as competitor or customer preference information, and say why it matters for DN's decision.

questions.issue: Some described objectives instead of reasons for change. Lack of developed analysis kept some at 6 marks or below.
questions.fix: Give two reasons why the objectives must change and take each one through a developed chain.

questions.topic: Importance of effective supply chain management
questions.issue: Some wrote vaguely about supply instead of the supply chain, or about physical goods and inventory.
questions.fix: Apply the idea to a business that provides online content, and end with a conclusion on how important it is to DN.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Both case contexts were well used, and most candidates answered all of the questions.
On the total costs calculation, most picked the correct figures and worked out total costs.
Most knew what just in time inventory management means.
Most could analyse how intrapreneurship would affect GT.
mistakes: Some wrote a paragraph or more for a one mark identify question.
Variable costs was a common wrong answer for direct costs, and answers that reused the words of the term were quite common.
Many used a sensible way to measure the size of GT but none of the data, which capped them at one mark.
Some gave only internet as a source of secondary research, and some confused primary and secondary use.
In the intrapreneurship question, answers often spent far longer analysing than evaluating, though evaluation carried 6 of the 12 marks.
A surprisingly high proportion weighed how important equality was to BB, when the question asked for its most likely impact.
fix: For identify questions, write a word or short phrase and move on.
Explain a term without reusing its own words, and cover every word in it, such as mass and customisation.
Use numbers from the data as context, for example a change in employee numbers.
Do not evaluate in an analyse question. Save judgement for part (d).
Set out calculation working in a clear order so the examiner can award each stage.

questions.issue: Variable costs was a common answer. Saying direct costs are costs directly related to production was quite common and earns nothing.
questions.fix: Show what makes a cost direct, then give an example to secure the application marks.

questions.issue: Some also worked out 2021, which was not needed. A common error was adding profit to revenue.
questions.fix: Total costs equal revenue minus profit. Work them out for 2020 and 2022, then find the change.

questions.issue: Many chose revenue or employees but did not use any of the given data.
questions.fix: Quote the figures, such as the fall in employee numbers, to apply your measure to GT.

questions.issue: Many began with a definition that was not needed. Internet alone was too vague.
questions.fix: Name specific sources that fit the case, such as past research by a hotel in the marina, and analyse their impact.

questions.issue: Attempts ranged from no judgement to many. Evaluation was often thin compared with the analysis.
questions.fix: Judge its importance to GT using the data, explain why without repeating your analysis, and say what the judgement depends on.

questions.issue: Many explained either mass or customisation, but rarely both. Some used the word customisation to explain itself.
questions.fix: Cover both parts in fresh words: changing some features to meet each customer's needs while producing large amounts of similar products. Then add an example.

questions.issue: Saying break-even is inaccurate was too vague to reward.
questions.fix: Say why it might be inaccurate, for example it relies on forecast data or assumes variable costs stay constant.

questions.topic: Impact of increased equality in the stitching department
questions.issue: Relatively few made a judgement on the most likely impact. Some knew only about equal pay.
questions.fix: Analyse more than one aspect of equality, then judge which impact on BB is most likely.

papers.title: Business concepts 2
well: Identifying an element of a business plan was very well answered.
Of those who knew how to work out the closing balance, the vast majority got all 3 marks.
Question 2 went well on the whole, with candidates showing solid knowledge of its topics.
Most could tell the production methods apart, and the question on changing CM's method went well.
Once a bank loan was defined specifically, candidates answered that question well.
mistakes: Many part (a) answers leaned on examples or lines lifted from the case, which earned nothing because part (a) tests knowledge only.
Many started a 12 mark answer with a one line judgement, which can earn at most one evaluation mark.
Variable costs explained without a link to output could not earn the application marks.
On digital promotion, many chose traditional methods only.
A significant minority forgot the market growth formula, and a significant minority described penetration pricing for price skimming.
Some analysed well in the production methods question but gave no judgement, losing all 6 evaluation marks.
fix: Answer part (a) from your own knowledge, not from the case.
Put your judgement at the end, after the analysis, and make it definite: should or should not.
Give each knowledge point its own piece of case application.
Learn the syllabus formulae and always show the working.
Write fewer chains of analysis, but develop each one fully.

questions.issue: Without linking the costs to output, the application marks for examples could not be given.
questions.fix: Say variable costs change with output, then give an example.

questions.topic: Human need satisfied by running JC
questions.issue: On occasion no human need was named. Two pieces of case detail were needed for application.
questions.fix: Name the need first, then use two specific facts about Jake and JC.

questions.issue: Some wrote about promotion in general without showing it is online. Many chose traditional methods only.
questions.fix: State that digital promotion is online, name an online method, and give each benefit its own case detail.

questions.topic: Bank loan as a source of finance for growth
questions.issue: Money borrowed from the bank was too general, since it could also mean an overdraft or mortgage.
questions.fix: Define a bank loan precisely, then reach a justified judgement in JC's context.

questions.issue: Definitions without a link to a given price were where candidates came unstuck.
questions.fix: Say it is the quantity customers are willing and able to buy at a given price, then show what can change it, such as incomes or the prices of substitutes.

questions.issue: A significant minority could not remember the formula.
questions.fix: Take the change in market sales, divide by the earlier figure and multiply by 100.

questions.issue: A significant minority described penetration pricing instead.
questions.fix: Learn that skimming starts with a high price, then apply that to CM.

questions.issue: Many relied on lots of short points. A pair of paragraphs saying should and should not is not a decision.
questions.fix: Finish with a final paragraph that clearly states whether CM should change and why.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: Some candidates clearly knew the new marking model well and came prepared for it.
Many correctly calculated the minimum project duration and the total float.
Many handled the technological change question quite well.
The strongest scripts knew the business concepts very well and backed them up with data from the case.
In Question 5, candidates clearly understood how a joint venture partner brings market knowledge.
mistakes: A significant number thought the change of structure meant becoming product orientated.
On critical path analysis, many did not mention the minimum project duration or total float, and there were generic answers.
Over half got the dividend cover wrong, usually by picking the wrong figures, for example earnings per share.
Very few used their dividend cover result when judging the annual report.
Some confused shareholders selling their own shares with the company issuing more shares.
Some confused a joint venture with a merger.
fix: Learn the published formula list. Some formulae, such as ARR, differ from older versions.
Spend the first 10 to 15 minutes reading the case so you know what the business does and who its customers are.
Use your earlier calculations as evidence in the later evaluate questions.
Write one clear paragraph for each of the two points in the 8 mark questions.
Consider other views too, such as whether it is the right time for the business to expand at all.

questions.topic: Advantages of changing to a product based organisational structure
questions.issue: A significant number misread this as the company becoming product orientated.
questions.fix: Analyse how teams for each paint product could focus on customer needs and make decisions faster.

questions.topic: Technological change and the nanopaints decision
questions.issue: Typical answers weighed the opportunity against the cost, though other angles such as marketing and distribution were also possible.
questions.fix: Write two clear paragraphs, for example the chance of a premium price against rivals catching up and the high development costs.

questions.issue: Many got it right, and stating the formula alone was worth one mark.
questions.fix: Use total float equals latest finish time minus duration minus earliest start time, and write the formula down.

questions.topic: Whether CPA will minimise interruption to production
questions.issue: This proved challenging. A number gave generic pros and cons of CPA without the case details, and many left out the project duration and total float.
questions.fix: Use your results from parts (a) and (b), and weigh the contractor's experience against risks like late component delivery.

questions.issue: More than half gave a wrong answer, typically from using the wrong figures, such as earnings per share. A few used the wrong year.
questions.fix: Check the year in the question, then divide profit for the year by the annual dividend.

questions.topic: Usefulness of the annual report to shareholders
questions.issue: Very few used their 4(a) answer. Some confused selling shares with the company raising finance.
questions.fix: Compare the forecast dividend cover with the previous year, then weigh falling profit and rising gearing against future plans.

questions.topic: Method of entering the market in country D
questions.issue: Some confused a joint venture with a merger, or were unclear how direct exporting to retailers would work.
questions.fix: Weigh the market knowledge of a joint venture against loss of control, and reach a clear choice for CP.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: On the economic environment question, many reached full marks by building two linked chains, each tied to CQ.
Most could pick out two of Frederico's leadership qualities, for example taking risks or inspiring others.
Among those who tried the NPV calculation, most scored well, usually 3 out of 4.
Candidates found the sustainability question approachable, and many evaluated in depth using CQ's context.
mistakes: Most got the capacity utilisation figure wrong, and a common slip was not expressing it as a percentage.
A significant number did not answer the inventory turnover question, and a few gave the wrong unit.
Some treated a rise in corporation tax as a rise in CQ's costs, which is wrong in accounting terms.
A few did not know what a leadership quality is and copied text from the case.
On lean production, few gave developed evaluation in context, and many suggested quality control the business already used.
On new product development, only a few added the second, separate line of evaluation needed for full marks.
fix: Show your method, use a calculator and give the correct unit with every answer.
Analyse only two impacts or qualities in Questions 1 and 2. Extra ones are not rewarded.
Make a brief plan before the 12 mark questions to keep answers focused.
Use your answers from earlier calculation parts as context in the evaluate questions.
Add evaluative comment at the end of each paragraph, then a justified final judgement.

questions.topic: Impact of two changes in the economic environment
questions.issue: A definition of the economic environment was not needed. Weaker answers made inaccurate claims about the tax change.
questions.fix: Link the weaker currency to the cost of imported bamboo. If you take the tax rise to be corporation tax, show that it cuts retained profit rather than raising costs.

questions.issue: Some analysed more than two qualities. A few copied phrases or whole paragraphs from the case.
questions.fix: Pick two qualities, such as being a good communicator, and chain each to CQ's success.

questions.issue: The majority calculated it incorrectly. Not giving the answer as a percentage was a common error.
questions.fix: Divide actual output by maximum capacity and multiply by 100, so the answer is a percentage and not a decimal.

questions.issue: A significant number did not answer. A few gave a wrong unit, such as dollars.
questions.fix: Use cost of sales divided by average inventory, show the working and give the answer in times.

questions.topic: Lean production and CQ's operational objectives
questions.issue: Few gave developed evaluation. Some ignored the operational objectives in the case.
questions.fix: Link JIT and quality circles or TQM to the case problems, then question whether they could work with CQ's supply issues and short time frame.

questions.issue: A significant number did not attempt it, and many did not deduct the capital cost.
questions.fix: Discount each year's cash flow, add them up, then subtract the capital cost.

questions.topic: Investing in measures to improve sustainability
questions.issue: This was handled well. The best answers weighed point against counterpoint throughout.
questions.fix: Use the NPV result, then set it against the mission statement and corporate social responsibility.

questions.topic: New product development and future success
questions.issue: Most stopped at a simple judgement. Only a few went on to a further strand of judgement for full evaluation marks.
questions.fix: Make your judgement in context, explain why, then add a second line of reasoning, such as the cash flow risk.

papers.title: Business decision-making
well: Candidates found the case very approachable, and nearly all of them reached the end of the paper.
Most answered the external constraints question effectively, showing they understood how outside changes could hold HP back.
Most showed their working on capacity utilisation and earned at least two of the three marks.
Candidates found the HRM strategy question approachable, and many answers were well organised, balanced and set in HP's context.
Many scripts were excellent, staying tightly on the question asked.
mistakes: A few analysed positive external changes, which earned nothing since the question asked about constraints.
Weaker answers wrote about single marketing tactics instead of the coordinated strategy.
A significant number did not attempt the percentage change in sales question.
On the factory modernisation, evaluation was often shallow or just went over earlier points again.
Some did not know the gearing formula or how to work out capital employed.
Weaker HRM answers were often one sided.
fix: Do not evaluate in Questions 1 and 2. They test analysis only.
Learn the full range of syllabus formulae, including gearing and income elasticity.
Use your answers to earlier calculation parts as evidence in the evaluate questions.
Give both sides even when the case leans one way, then make a supported judgement.
Allow about 1.5 minutes per mark, so roughly 18 minutes for a 12 mark answer.

questions.topic: Constraints from changes in the external environment
questions.issue: A few wrote about more than two changes or about positive ones.
questions.fix: Use two constraints from the case, such as new multinational rivals and higher interest rates, one per paragraph.

questions.topic: Benefits of a coordinated marketing strategy
questions.issue: Weaker answers described separate tactics, not how the strategy fits together.
questions.fix: Show how the parts of the mix support each other, for example making the promotion budget go further.

questions.issue: Some did not know the formula but earned a mark for the forecast maximum capacity.
questions.fix: Work out the 2024 maximum capacity first, then divide forecast output by it and multiply by 100.

questions.issue: A significant number did not attempt it, and many did not know how to use the data.
questions.fix: Multiply the change in incomes by the income elasticity of demand.

questions.issue: Weaker responses never mentioned efficiency. Evaluation was often superficial.
questions.fix: Judge what success depends on, such as accurate sales forecasts, reliable machines and training, using capacity utilisation as context.

questions.issue: Of the three calculations, this caused the most trouble. Some lacked the gearing formula, and some could not work out capital employed.
questions.fix: Divide non-current liabilities by capital employed and multiply by 100. Capital employed is equity plus non-current liabilities.

questions.topic: Using financial data to choose how to finance the modernisation
questions.issue: Weaker answers debated whether to modernise at all. Some wrongly assumed a highly geared firm cannot borrow more.
questions.fix: Link one or two pieces of data to sources such as shares, retained profit or loans, for example how gearing would change.

questions.issue: Weaker responses were often one sided.
questions.fix: Balance benefits such as delegation and motivated staff with the cost of training and rivals poaching skilled staff.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Successful responses picked two or three marketing activities and weighed what worked and what did not.
The stronger Question 2 answers covered at least two outside influences and weighed whether each would help PV succeed or hold it back.
mistakes: Weaker answers often just retold the case, at times copying it out with no analysis added.
Some wrote about things that were not marketing, such as company status, lean production, training or gearing.
Some suggested alternative or future marketing instead of judging what had already happened.
Some used SWOT, Ansoff or PESTLE, or tools like Blue Ocean and the Boston matrix, which did not fit the question.
Weaker answers on external influences listed them all without saying how they affect PV.
Some wrote as if the electric vehicle strategy had already happened.
fix: Stay inside the time period the question gives. Earlier activity earns no analysis or evaluation marks.
For each activity, give a developed benefit and a developed counterpoint to reach the top analysis level.
Match each external influence to a PEST heading, then say how far it would affect PV.
Back your final judgement with case evidence and your earlier analysis.
Plan your time: about 15 minutes reading and planning, then about 30 minutes per question.

questions.topic: Evaluating PV's marketing strategy from 2012 to 2021
questions.issue: Some went outside the period or outside marketing, and some offered future plans instead of judging the past.
questions.fix: Take two or three activities, such as specialist magazine adverts or the TV features, and judge their success with evidence.

questions.topic: External influences on PV's future strategy
questions.issue: Some listed every influence with no effect on PV. Others analysed strategic approaches instead of influences.
questions.fix: Choose two or three influences, analyse positive and negative effects in chains, and judge the extent of each.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Some answers analysed the likeliest effects of FL's corporate culture well.
Some top answers chose the culture's two largest impacts and looked at the good and bad side of each.
mistakes: Many tried to analyse every item in the timeline instead of choosing the most important.
Some showed no knowledge of corporate culture and judged FL's overall success instead.
The majority gave no judgement on whether blue ocean strategy was the most useful approach.
A significant number showed no knowledge of blue ocean strategy and scored zero on that question.
Some wrote about whether FL should diversify, which was not the question.
Some spent too long on one question and left only an outline for the other.
fix: Start from the theory in the question, such as corporate culture, and keep every paragraph tied to it.
Be selective with the data. Choose the most relevant parts.
Compare blue ocean with one other approach and judge which is more useful.
Aim for 25 to 30 minutes per question with three or four good chains of analysis.
Give a clear decision, justify it and weigh what else might change it.

questions.topic: Impact of corporate culture on FL's success
questions.issue: Some judged FL's success overall, which was not rewarded. Some used data without linking it to culture.
questions.fix: Define corporate culture, pick its two biggest impacts, such as home working or the culture clash with GY, and judge which mattered more.

questions.topic: Blue ocean strategy as the most useful approach
questions.issue: The majority made no judgement on blue ocean. Calling another approach useful did not answer the question unless compared with blue ocean.
questions.fix: Analyse blue ocean's benefits and costs, or set it against one other approach, then judge whether it is the most useful.

papers.title: Business strategy
well: Question 1, on operations strategy, went well on the whole.
On the whole, candidates understood operations strategies well and tied them to RT's business.
Most Question 2 answers earned every knowledge mark.
Most candidates finished both questions in the time.
mistakes: A general definition of operations strategy, or a bare list of methods, earned no knowledge marks.
Many strong responses gave no context in their evaluation or no second judgement, so stopped at 6 of 7.
Some answered Question 2 with diversification methods or marketing ideas, which earned no marks.
Some named PEST without defining it, so gained no knowledge mark.
In Question 2, much of the analysis stopped at Level 1 and was never developed further.
fix: Define each specific strategy you use, such as lean production, JIT or Kaizen.
Focus on two or three aspects so you have time to develop each chain.
Give a counterargument with its own chain of reasoning, and do it twice.
After your judgement, add what it depends on, in context, to reach full evaluation marks.
Spell out what each approach stands for and how it works before applying it.

questions.issue: Many strong scripts lost the last evaluation mark by not adding a second judgement or context.
questions.fix: Judge clearly whether the operations strategy supported success, then add what that depends on in RT's context.

questions.topic: Approaches to developing a strategy for profit through diversification
questions.issue: Responses were weaker than in Question 1. Some focused on diversification itself rather than the strategic approaches.
questions.fix: Discuss at least two approaches, such as SWOT and Ansoff, then pick one and explain why it best suits RT.

quote.text: Development of the information given in the question is necessary

takeaways: Give every figure its correct, up to date label. Right numbers lost marks under wrong labels, and old terms like net profit are not accepted.
Finish every working with a net figure. A bracket of additions and multiplications with no answer at the end earns no calculation mark.
When a question offers two options, comment on both before you choose. Talking only about your chosen option caps your marks.
Build on the scenario instead of copying it back, and never stop at one or two words when the command word is explain.
In the A Level papers, balance your advice: give reasons for and against, bring in other factors, then decide.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: 51 per cent of candidates got 15 or more questions right.
Questions 2 and 19 were straightforward, with 78 and 91 per cent choosing the key.
In question 15 most candidates correctly ruled out the two options containing statement 1.
mistakes: In question 6 many chose D, a pair of errors that would actually stop the trial balance agreeing.
In question 8 some took the bank charges off a second time, although the adjusted statement figure already allowed for them.
In question 12 almost half picked an answer equal to the new monthly rent of $1100.
In question 16 some deducted the partner's loan interest again, though the profit figure given was already after it.
In question 26 many chose D, the option without inventory valuation, even though absorption costing is an accepted way to value inventory.
fix: On bank questions, check your choice by drafting a quick reconciliation.
In trial balance and suspense questions, follow each entry from its book of prime entry to the ledger account it reaches.
Know what each costing method is good for and where it falls short, for example absorption costing in inventory valuation.
In appropriation questions, check whether each figure has already been taken off before the profit you are given.

questions.topic: Which error would not affect the trial balance totals
questions.issue: Many chose D and some chose C. Only some chose the key A.
questions.fix: A wrong figure in the book of prime entry is carried into both ledger entries, so the totals still agree.

questions.issue: Some chose B by deducting the $124 bank charges. Almost a third chose the key, $5858 debit.
questions.fix: Start from the $8360 statement balance, add the uncredited cheques and take off the unpresented ones. The charges are already in that figure.

questions.issue: Almost half chose C or D, which use only the new rent of $1100.
questions.fix: Add the $1000 brought forward to the $13 000 received, take off $1100 paid in advance for January 2023, and compare $12 900 with the $13 000 shown.

questions.issue: Of those rejecting statement 1, most chose C, perhaps forgetting that current account credit balances are also owed to partners. 30 per cent chose the key D.
questions.fix: Capital accounts alone do not show everything owed to a partner. Together, capital and current accounts equal net assets.

questions.issue: Fewer than half chose the key B. Some chose A by deducting the loan interest again.
questions.fix: Take only X's $10 000 salary from $150 000, then give Z one fifth of the rest, $28 000.

questions.issue: Many chose D, and half of candidates split equally between C and the key A.
questions.fix: All three statements are true: it values inventory, sets prices by adding profit to total cost, and includes all production costs.

papers.title: Multiple choice
well: More than half of candidates scored 17 or more.
Questions 1, 10, 17 and 27 were straightforward, and a significant number chose the key.
None of the 30 questions caused serious trouble.
mistakes: In question 3 almost half missed that the bank balance was only $1000, so drawings of $2000 by cheque created an overdraft.
In question 13, those choosing C most likely mishandled items 2 and 4, possibly reversing a wrong entry without completing the correction.
In question 18 about as many chose A as the key, multiplying the new shares by the premium alone.
In question 26 over a third chose C, which describes a cost unit, instead of the key D.
fix: Read every detail in the question, such as an opening bank balance, before you apply a transaction.
To correct an error, cancel the wrong entry and then post the right one. Do both steps.
Cash from a share issue is the number of new shares times the nominal value plus the premium.
Learn exact costing definitions: a cost centre is a location, while a cost unit is what costs are worked out for.

questions.topic: Accounting equation after drawings and a credit purchase
questions.issue: Almost 50 per cent chose A. About one third chose the key C.
questions.fix: Drawings can only empty the $1000 bank, so the other $1000 becomes an overdraft. Then add $3000 of inventory and payables.

questions.issue: About a third chose either C or the key A. C is $4200 above the key, most likely from mishandling items 2 and 4.
questions.fix: For items 2 and 4, cancel the wrong amount and post the right one: $149 000 less 2500, 2100, 1200 and 6000, plus 5100, gives $142 300.

questions.topic: Cash raised by a rights issue
questions.issue: 85 per cent chose A or the key C in an equal split. A used only the $1.50 premium.
questions.fix: Find the 75 000 new shares, then multiply by $3.50, the $2 nominal value plus the premium, to get $262 500.

questions.topic: Describing a cost centre rather than a cost unit
questions.issue: Over a third chose C instead of the key D.
questions.fix: A cost centre is any location where costs are incurred. A part of a product for which costs are calculated is a cost unit.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: In 1(e) most named the current ratio and the acid test ratio as liquidity measures.
Revenue reserves in 3(a) were well answered, often citing dividends and everyday trading.
Those who attempted the rights issue in 3(b) usually earned all three marks.
Those who attempted the overhead apportionment in 4(a) mostly scored well.
mistakes: In 1(a) some used the wrong years of ownership and found a profit instead of the $1800 loss.
In 1(c) weaker candidates struggled with the adjustments and seldom passed five marks.
In 2(b) the most common error was naming the sales ledger, not the journal, for irrecoverable debts written off.
In 4(b) many ignored two decimal places or left out per machine hour or per labour hour.
In 4(e) many could not handle production at 80 per cent of factory capacity.
In 4(g) only a few earned more than three of the seven marks, as answers were vague.
fix: Count exactly how many years an asset was owned before you work out its depreciation to the date of sale.
In a control account, label money from credit customers as bank, not receipts.
Round absorption rates to two decimal places and always write per machine hour or per labour hour.
A 25 per cent profit margin means adding one third of total cost, as the mark scheme does in 4(c).
Practise past advice questions on new products, so you weigh financial and non-financial points.

questions.issue: Some miscounted the years of ownership and showed a profit.
questions.fix: In the scheme, three years at 25 per cent of $28 000 leaves $7000. Against proceeds of $5200 that is a loss of $1800.

questions.topic: Improving the rate of inventory turnover
questions.issue: Some made valid points but never actually advised Mima.
questions.fix: Give points on both options, then a clear choice. The scheme gives a mark for a supported decision.

questions.issue: The sales ledger was often given for irrecoverable debts.
questions.fix: Irrecoverable debts written off are recorded first in the journal.

questions.topic: Revised sales ledger control account balance
questions.issue: Only a very small minority finished it fully.
questions.fix: Only errors that change totals affect the control account. In the scheme, add the omitted $820 invoice and deduct the $470 understated returns.

questions.issue: Figures were often right, but rounding and the per hour basis were missing.
questions.fix: Give each rate to two decimal places with its basis, for example per machine hour.

questions.issue: Many got the costs right, but some struggled to turn the margin into a mark-up.
questions.fix: Total the materials, labour and overheads, then add one third of that cost for a 25 per cent margin on price.

questions.issue: Many could not use the 80 per cent capacity level.
questions.fix: Take 80 per cent of 28 000 labour hours, divide by 2.5 hours a unit, multiply by the $13 contribution and deduct fixed costs.

questions.topic: Advice on making the new product
questions.issue: Answers were often vague and lacked focus.
questions.fix: Give points for and against, financial and non-financial, such as repeat orders and lost regular customers, then decide.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: Several scripts were strong, and financial statements were well presented in many.
In 1(c) most earned the mark for a valid reason to make a bonus issue.
In 1(f) most weighed both options and reached a supported decision.
In 3(d) most scored both marks by naming the cost and the time of keeping full records.
mistakes: In 1(a) abbreviations such as COS and old labels such as net profit lost marks.
In 1(b) the most common error was leaving out the dividend paid.
In 1(d) some missed that a bonus issue involves no cash and said it would help repay liabilities.
In 2(b) very few got full marks, mostly because of wrong labels in the cash book.
In 3(a), trying to build a statement of profit or loss to find the result rarely worked.
In 4(f)(ii) the most common mistake was the overtime payment.
fix: Write labels in full and in current terms: cost of sales, gross profit, profit for the year.
In the cash book, label each entry with the account it goes to.
With incomplete records, compare closing capital with opening capital plus capital introduced less drawings. The gap is the profit or loss.
Revise the layout of a bank reconciliation statement from your earlier studies.
In advice questions, add judgement and non-financial points instead of repeating the question.

questions.issue: Labels were incomplete or wrong, such as COS or net profit.
questions.fix: Use full current labels, and end with profit for the year.

questions.topic: Retained earnings after a bonus issue
questions.issue: Good workings helped, but the dividend paid was often missed.
questions.fix: From the opening balance, add profit, then deduct the dividend paid and the part of the bonus issue taken from retained earnings.

questions.topic: Why lenders might approve of a bonus issue
questions.issue: Many found it hard, and some implied the issue brought in cash to repay debts.
questions.fix: No cash leaves or enters the company, so its ability to repay what it owes is unchanged.

questions.issue: Many had forgotten the structure and produced confused statements.
questions.fix: Start from the updated cash book balance, adjust for the unpresented cheques and the outstanding bankings, and end at the bank statement balance.

questions.topic: Profit or loss from incomplete records
questions.issue: Overall performance was not satisfactory.
questions.fix: Find closing capital from assets less liabilities, then compare it with $41 000 plus the $9000 vehicle less drawings. The scheme shows a loss.

questions.issue: A common error was misusing the opening and closing inventory.
questions.fix: Opening inventory for 2022 is the $18 450 closing figure for 2021. Find cost of sales, then multiply by 1.5 for a 50 per cent mark-up.

questions.issue: Well prepared candidates got all six marks, but overtime pay was often wrong.
questions.fix: Pay normal hours at the basic rate and only the extra hours at the overtime rate. The scheme uses 14 000 hours at $18 and 1400 at $27.

questions.issue: Many repeated the question with no evaluation and stayed at two or three marks.
questions.fix: Consider financial and non-financial factors for both options, then decide. Several candidates who did this got all seven.

papers.title: Fundamentals of accounting
well: In 1(a) many correctly named the prudence concept for damaged inventory.
In 4(b) most calculated the break-even point in units and in sales value correctly.
In 4(e) many answered well, pointing to the option with the highest profit and the capacity effect of each.
In 3(d) many gave valid reasons to cut dividends, such as falling profits and a lack of liquid funds.
mistakes: Right values often carried the wrong label, especially in the statement of profit or loss and in journals.
In 1(c) rent was often reduced by $1700 instead of increased by two months' rent of $3400.
In 1(c) depreciation was rarely right, because the $6500 of new equipment was not taken out before the full year charge.
In 2(b) the $90 difference was often used for error 2 instead of the full $770.
In 3(b) some based the 2021 dividend on a $1 share instead of $0.50.
In 4(c) many took 25 per cent off the old net price of $16 instead of off the price before any discount.
fix: Always end a working with its net value.
In any advice question with two options, comment on both before you choose.
Deduct the irrecoverable debt from receivables before you work out the allowance.
Round a break-even point up to the next whole unit.
For an error of principle, say the entry went to the wrong class of account, with the correct amount on the correct side.

questions.topic: Statement of profit or loss adjustments
questions.issue: Very few were fully correct. Rent and depreciation caused most trouble.
questions.fix: Rent is $17 000 plus two thirds of $5100, so $20 400. Depreciation is 20 per cent of $29 500 plus the $650 on the new equipment.

questions.issue: Few mentioned the aim of raising gross profit, and some discussed only their chosen option.
questions.fix: Cover storage and quality for option A and advertising and price for option B, then choose.

questions.issue: Error 1 was often reversed, and in error 4 the credit named a customer in general instead of W Limited.
