questions.fix: For error 2, $340 should have been credited but $430 was debited, so correct by $770. Name W Limited for error 4.

questions.issue: Many left out the opening entry for the $700 difference.
questions.fix: Debits exceeded credits by $700, so the suspense account opens with a $700 credit.

questions.issue: Many did not work back to the position before the issue.
questions.fix: The issue was two fifths of the $1 000 000 shares, $400 000. Put 60 per cent back to share premium and 40 per cent back to retained earnings.

questions.issue: Some used $1 shares for 2021, and some did not say whether the dividend rose or fell.
questions.fix: 20 per cent of $3600 nominal gives $720. 12 000 shares at $0.05 gives $600, a fall of $120.

questions.topic: Increase in the margin of safety
questions.issue: Material price, monthly fixed costs and rounding caused errors, and the current margin was often missing.
questions.fix: The list price was $20, so the new price is $15. Use monthly fixed costs, round break-even up, and compare old and new margins.

questions.issue: Regular customers' units were not reduced, and the new order was priced at $26 instead of $24.
questions.fix: Regular sales fall to 13 800 units. The new order earns $5.50 a unit after the lower price and packaging.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Performance was good overall, and question 3 scored best of the three.
The working capital cycle in 2(c)(i) was very well done, with many fully correct and nearly everyone rounding each part up as told.
3(b) produced very good manufacturing accounts, with a significant number fully correct.
Both retained earnings parts, 2(b)(ii) and 2(b)(iii), were well answered.
mistakes: In 1(a) some piled extra items on top of the residual profit they were given.
In the capital accounts for 1(b), part of the current accounts went missing, or the trade payables discount or goodwill was mishandled, so the realisation profit came out wrong.
In 1(c) the errors came almost always from working out the purchase consideration.
The partnership bank account in 1(d) was weak: trade payables or the cash from J Limited were left out, and a few reversed the partners' entries.
In 2(d) most advised and gave reasons for concern, but very few gave reasons the directors need not worry.
In 3(c) finished goods inventory was valued at cost, factory profit was missed, or the rise in the provision for unrealised profit was treated wrongly.
fix: In 1(a) the profit is only the interest on capital plus the residual profit. Add nothing else.
Work out the consideration first: assets taken over plus goodwill. Then take off the debentures and shares to find the cash.
In a statement of profit or loss after a manufacturing account, value finished goods at transfer value, so factory profit is included.
When you name the prudence concept, also say how it applies to the inventory in the question.
In advice answers, go beyond two points and add the other side before you decide. In 1(e), few passed three marks.

questions.issue: Some added unrelated items to the residual profit.
questions.fix: In the scheme, profit is the partners' interest on capital plus the residual profit, $62 000.

questions.issue: A limited number were fully correct. Current account items were missed and the discount or goodwill was mishandled.
questions.fix: Bring in each partner's current account balance and build the realisation profit from assets, goodwill and the trade payables discount.

questions.topic: Cash paid in by J Limited
questions.issue: Most dealt correctly with the debentures and shares, but the consideration itself was often wrong.
questions.fix: Consideration is the value of assets taken over plus goodwill, $694 000 in the scheme. Deduct debentures and shares to leave the cash.

questions.issue: Trade payables or the payment from J Limited were left out, and a few reversed the partners' entries.
questions.fix: Include the trade payables paid, the cash from J Limited you found in (c) and the final payments to each partner.

questions.issue: Some stopped at non-current assets and earned one mark, and a few multiplied revenue by the non-current asset turnover.
questions.fix: Divide revenue by the turnover to get non-current assets, add the current assets, then deduct trade payables and the debenture.

questions.issue: The usual slip was inventory turnover, often because cost of sales or average inventory was wrong.
questions.fix: Find cost of sales from revenue and the gross margin, work out opening inventory, then average it with closing inventory.

questions.topic: Concern about the working capital cycle
questions.issue: Very few balanced their advice with reasons not to be concerned.
questions.fix: Add points such as the difference not being material or the firms having different policies, then decide.

questions.topic: Statement of profit or loss with factory profit
questions.issue: Only a few were fully correct. Inventories at cost and the unrealised profit adjustment caused most errors.
questions.fix: Value opening and closing finished goods with their mark-up, add factory profit and deduct the increase in the provision for unrealised profit.

papers.title: Financial accounting
well: Question 1 was the best answered on this paper.
1(a), the cafe account, was generally well set out, and some were fully correct.
The realisation account in 3(b) was a strength, and a significant number got every entry right.
The journal entries in 3(d) were generally well prepared, with some earning full marks.
mistakes: In 1(a) wages were not added back, giving the wrong revenue, and the cafe equipment depreciation was miscalculated.
In 1(c) a significant number did not attempt it, and many missed the opening bank balance or the life membership balances.
In 1(d) some brought shareholders and dilution of control into a club's choice of loan.
In 2(a) very few calculated the depreciation that was missed or said it was a change in accounting policy.
In 2(c) very few got profit from operations right, and many left out the purchase of the machine.
In 3(c) very few worked out the current account balances to transfer, which cost four marks.
fix: Read how the cafe takings were recorded. The scheme adds the $14 400 of wages to $55 000 to reach revenue.
For the opening accumulated fund, include the bank balance and deduct the life membership balances not yet credited to income.
Learn IAS 8: a prior period adjustment is made against retained earnings brought forward.
In acquisition journals, split the share issue into share capital and share premium, and work out goodwill.
Tie your advice to the people and facts in the question, not a general list.

questions.issue: Revenue was wrong when wages were not added back.
questions.fix: Revenue in the scheme is $55 000 plus the $14 400 wages, and equipment depreciation is 20 per cent of $30 800.

questions.issue: The most common error was leaving out the loss on sale of club equipment.
questions.fix: Include the $2800 loss on sale of club equipment as expenditure.

questions.issue: Very few were fully correct, though most added their surplus at the end.
questions.fix: Opening fund is the given balances plus the bank less the life membership still deferred. Then add the surplus.

questions.topic: Advice on a loan to buy premises
questions.issue: Most gave valid points, but some wrote about shareholders.
questions.fix: Compare the bank loan and the member's loan on security, interest rate, speed and whether it can be recalled.

questions.issue: A limited number named the standard, and very few found the missing depreciation.
questions.fix: State the $20 000 depreciation missed for 2021, that it is a change in accounting policy under IAS 8, and that it goes to retained earnings brought forward.

questions.issue: Hardly anyone added the prior period adjustment, and relatively few got both dividends right.
questions.fix: Start from the rise in retained earnings, then add back the prior period adjustment, the 2021 final dividend and the 2022 interim dividend.

questions.issue: Layout was generally good, but profit from operations and the machine purchase were often wrong.
questions.fix: Profit from operations is profit for the year plus interest. Put the machine purchase under investing activities.

questions.issue: Very few found the current account balances, but most entered the opening balances, realisation profit and shares.
questions.fix: Net assets at book value less the capital accounts gives the current account total. The scheme splits it two thirds to Alice and one third to Bob.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Results were good overall, with question 1 the strongest.
Many handled the net present value in 1(a)(i) well, and a significant number were fully correct.
Most found the payback period in 1(a)(ii) correctly, including some who slipped in the part before.
2(d), the trade payables budget, was generally good, and own figure marks helped those with an earlier slip.
mistakes: In 1(a)(i) the usual error was spreading the proceeds evenly over the four years instead of following how the dig progressed.
In 1(a)(iii) the payment to the farmer was left out of average profit, or total investment was used instead of average investment.
In 1(b) many judged each appraisal method, but relatively few brought in other factors, so only a few passed four marks.
The most common error in 2(a) was ignoring the production constraints, which meant April demand could not be fully met.
In 2(b) few saw that the production limit had to be used for April revenue, so very few got more than one mark.
In 2(d) the most common error was splitting the payments to suppliers wrongly between months.
fix: Time each cash inflow as the source describes. Do not spread it evenly unless the question says so.
For ARR, divide average profit by average investment. In the scheme, average investment is half of the $100 000 cost.
After commenting on each method, add other factors such as risk and how uncertain the proceeds are.
Budgeted revenue can only come from units that can actually be made, so check the constraint for every month.
In a trade payables budget, show how much of each month's purchases is paid that month and how much is carried to the next.

questions.topic: Net present value of the dig
questions.issue: The most common error was equal proceeds each year.
questions.fix: Place each year's proceeds in line with the progress of the dig, then apply the discount factors.

questions.issue: Some forgot the payment to the farmer or used the total investment.
questions.fix: Use total profit over four years divided by 4, over the average investment of $50 000. The scheme gets 22.5 per cent.

questions.topic: Advice on going ahead with the dig
questions.issue: Many gave a point on each method but few looked wider.
questions.fix: Add risk factors from the scheme, such as uncertain finds and prices, then give a supported decision.

questions.issue: Nearly all gave one disadvantage, and only some gave a second.
questions.fix: The scheme accepts that ARR ignores the time value of money and ignores the timing of cash flows.

questions.issue: The constraints were often ignored.
questions.fix: Cap production at the monthly limit and let closing inventory fall, so you can see where April demand goes unmet.

questions.issue: Many explained reasonably but missed the production constraint.
questions.fix: Say revenue is units sold times selling price, and that April sales are limited by what can be produced.

questions.issue: The split of payments between months was often wrong.
questions.fix: Start with opening payables, add purchases, then deduct last month's balance paid and this month's share paid.

questions.topic: Effect of a discount on budgeted profit
questions.issue: Many said profit would rise, and only some linked it to the discount received.
questions.fix: Say the statement gains an entry for discount received, which raises budgeted profit by 2 per cent of purchases.

papers.title: Cost and management accounting
well: Results were good, and question 1 drew the strongest answers.
A high number scored all four marks on the net present value in 1(b), helped by credit for correct factors on own figures.
Most knew the ARR formula in 1(a)(ii) and applied it correctly.
In 2(a) a high number calculated the sales price variance and the fixed overhead expenditure variance correctly.
mistakes: In 1(a)(i) a very common error was missing the income from the extra eighty houses in years 3 and 4.
In 1(c) the year 3 and 4 cash flows were often wrong, and some found a new NPV without stating the change and its direction.
In 1(d) most used their NPV and ARR, but very few earned the other marks.
In 2(a) many did not get the actual profit, although it could be worked out from the results given.
In 2(c) relatively few saw that more hours had been worked, and some answers ignored the scenario.
In 2(d) many gave no calculations, which held them to four marks.
fix: Show the cash flow for each year and the total for the project.
Give ARR as a percentage to two decimal places.
When asked for a change, subtract the two figures and say whether it is an increase or a decrease.
Tie each variance reason to the business in the question.
When advice must be supported with calculations, include them, or you lose those marks.

questions.topic: Net cash flow of the project
questions.issue: Income from the extra houses in years 3 and 4 was often missed, and some gave no total.
questions.fix: Build the fees year by year from the source, then add the years to give the project total.

questions.issue: A few showed a negative NPV as positive or the reverse.
questions.fix: Keep the sign of each discounted flow. Correct factors applied to your own figures still earn full credit.

questions.topic: Change in NPV with the extension
questions.issue: Year 3 and 4 flows were often wrong, and the change and its direction were sometimes missing.
questions.fix: In the scheme the NPV falls from $1926 to negative $566, a decrease of $2492. State the word decrease.

questions.topic: Advice on the sea wall and extension
questions.issue: Answers leaned on NPV and ARR, and very few added the wider points the scheme also credits.
questions.fix: Add points on risk, estimated figures and Hiram's links to the village, then decide.

questions.issue: Performance varied, and the actual profit was often wrong.
questions.fix: Work each variance with its favourable or adverse label, and calculate actual profit from the results provided.

questions.topic: Reason for the material price variance
questions.issue: A high number named the fall in price, and only some developed it.
questions.fix: Say the market price fell and give a reason, such as lower demand for non recyclable material.

questions.topic: Reason for the labour efficiency variance
questions.issue: Relatively few saw that more hours were worked.
questions.fix: Link the extra hours to the scenario, such as a cut in the hourly rate leaving workers demotivated.

questions.topic: Advice on switching to recyclable material
questions.issue: Many gave no calculations, so four marks was the limit.
questions.fix: Show how the $24 per kg material changes profit, then give comments and a decision.

quote.text: only explained points will gain credit for analysis

takeaways: Evaluation means weighing your analysis and reaching a judgement. A recap of points you already made does not count.
Explain each step in your chain of reasoning. Stating an effect without saying why it happens earns little.
When a diagram is asked for, draw it, label the axes exactly, and explain it in words.
Read every key word: most immediate, always, after tax, definitely. Several reports show marks lost by answering a nearby question.
Cover the whole syllabus. On Paper 23 very few tried the circular flow question, an area the report calls new, and most who did scored very low.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: Questions 3 and 6 were answered best, by 75 per cent or more.
Micro and macro questions were handled equally well.
mistakes: Almost half of the questions were answered correctly by fewer than half of candidates.
In question 9, 36 per cent picked an option that only said quantity reacts to price, missing the revenue link.
In question 13, 37 per cent blamed inelastic short run supply for the excess demand.
fix: Link price elasticity of demand to total revenue: if demand is price elastic, a price cut raises revenue.
Excess demand comes from a price held below equilibrium. Inelastic supply alone just gives a higher equilibrium price.
Look for what the question is really testing, and reject options that are partly true but miss it.

questions.issue: One of the two best answered questions, at 75 per cent or above.
questions.fix: Keep the meaning sharp: the gain from paying less than the most you were willing to pay.

questions.issue: Only 24 per cent were right, while 36 per cent chose A.
questions.fix: Price elastic demand means a price fall raises total revenue, which is option D.

questions.issue: 32 per cent chose the key C, and 37 per cent chose D.
questions.fix: A price fixed below equilibrium causes the shortage. With inelastic supply the market would still settle at an equilibrium.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: 60 per cent of questions were answered correctly by 60 per cent or more of candidates.
Questions 7, 16 and 18 were answered best, by 81 per cent or above.
Neither the micro nor the macro questions stood out as harder.
mistakes: Only 29 per cent picked out the incentive function of price in question 5, and 30 per cent chose A.
In question 11, 30 per cent chose the option saying supply grows more inelastic as price rises, the reverse of the key.
In question 25, 51 per cent assumed inflation would definitely change the terms of trade.
Only 36 per cent worked out the change in rice output after specialisation in question 26.
fix: Learn the functions of price. The incentive function is about producers choosing to stay in or leave a market.
For a supply curve starting on the quantity axis, PES is perfectly inelastic at a zero price and rises as price rises.
Treat words like definitely as a test: something that only might happen is not the answer.
Find each country's opportunity cost, decide who specialises in what, then compare world output before and after.

questions.issue: Only 29 per cent were right, and 30 per cent chose A.
questions.fix: Option B fits, because a price fall pushes some producers out of the market.

questions.topic: Price elasticity of supply along a curve
questions.issue: 33 per cent chose the key D, and 30 per cent chose the opposite, C.
questions.fix: At a zero price with positive quantity, PES is zero. It then rises as you move up the curve.

questions.topic: What definitely changes the terms of trade
questions.issue: 51 per cent chose A and only 25 per cent the key C.
questions.fix: Inflation may leave export prices unchanged, so it is not certain to change the terms of trade. Statements 1 and 3 are certain.

questions.issue: The question was found difficult, and only 36 per cent chose C.
questions.fix: N specialises in rice and M in wheat. Rice output goes from 70 to 75, a gain of 5 units.

papers.title: AS Level multiple choice
well: Questions 2, 3, 4 and 6 were answered best, at 70 per cent or above.
91 per cent got question 4 on the conditions that encourage enterprise.
Performance on micro and macro items was much the same.
mistakes: Only 27 per cent saw in question 10 that equal 5 per cent falls in price and revenue mean PED is zero.
In question 15, 61 per cent chose the revenue before tax when the question asked for after tax.
Only 6 per cent got question 17 right, and 39 per cent chose net secondary income.
In question 23, 41 per cent had the two countries' specialisations the wrong way round.
fix: If revenue falls by the same percentage as price, quantity has not changed, so demand is perfectly inelastic.
For a tax on a firm, find revenue at the new equilibrium, then take off the tax paid.
Work out each country's opportunity cost before you decide who makes what.
Learn the four current account headings in the syllabus: goods, services, primary income and secondary income.

questions.topic: PED from a price and revenue change
questions.issue: 27 per cent chose the key D.
questions.fix: A 5 per cent price fall with a 5 per cent revenue fall means quantity is unchanged, so PED is zero.

questions.topic: After tax revenue of a firm
questions.issue: Only 24 per cent chose the key A, and 61 per cent chose B, the revenue before tax.
questions.fix: Take total revenue at the new price, then deduct the total tax paid. The answer is $100.

questions.topic: Remittances in Qatar's balance of payments
questions.issue: Only 6 per cent chose the key B, and 39 per cent chose secondary income.
questions.fix: The key is B. The report classes these wages sent home as primary income, so learn that classification for this question.

questions.issue: Only 20 per cent chose the key C, and 41 per cent chose D.
questions.fix: X has the lower opportunity cost in shoes, so X makes shoes and Y makes T shirts. Total output becomes 24 000.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: In 1(a) many calculated the change in India's unemployment rate correctly.
In 1(b) a number used the data well to explain seasonal unemployment from farming.
In 2(a) most drew a suitable diagram showing a movement along and a shift of the PPC.
In 5(b) many showed good knowledge and analysis of the arguments for and against protectionism.
mistakes: In 1(a) some described each month instead of the change over the whole period.
Evaluation was thin in 1(c), 1(d) and 1(e): very few tried it in 1(c), and many skipped it in 1(e) despite the word assess.
In 2(b) some assumed education must be a public good because governments provide it.
In 3(a) some XED formulas left out percentage changes or put the price change on top.
In 4(a) some labelled the axes price and quantity and the curves D and S, instead of AD/AS terms.
fix: Spot the command word first: calculate, explain, consider or assess, and answer that.
For XED, put the percentage change in quantity demanded of one good over the percentage change in price of the other.
Label AD/AS axes as price level and real GDP or output, and the curves as AD and AS.
Label the vertical axis of a currency diagram as the exchange rate or price of the currency.
Four of the twelve marks in part (b) are for evaluation, so weigh the arguments and reach a judgement.

questions.issue: Some listed month by month changes instead of one overall change.
questions.fix: Compare the two end points, 7.4 and 11.9 per cent. Either 4.5 or 60.81 per cent was accepted.

questions.issue: Very few evaluated, and some wrote about measurement methods instead.
questions.fix: Use difficulties such as inactive or discouraged workers and the informal economy, then judge how far they matter.

questions.issue: Many gave no evaluation despite the word assess.
questions.fix: Weigh fiscal, monetary and supply-side measures against each other, then decide.

questions.topic: Movement along and shift of a PPC
questions.issue: Some curves did not meet the axes, some drew demand and supply, and some judged the most significant effect, not the most immediate.
questions.fix: Draw the PPC touching both axes, link a movement to opportunity cost, and judge which has the most immediate impact.

questions.topic: Education as a public good or merit good
questions.issue: A number wrote about public sector provision instead of the distinction asked for.
questions.fix: A public good is non rival and non excludable. A merit good is a private good that is rival and excludable.

questions.issue: Formulas were sometimes wrong, and few weighed which determinants matter most.
questions.fix: Write the formula with percentage changes, explain substitutes and complements, then judge the most important determinant.

questions.issue: Answers were often descriptive, and some diagrams had the wrong axis or curve labels.
questions.fix: Label the diagram fully, then say in what circumstances one type is more damaging.

questions.issue: Many labelled the vertical axis as price, and few judged whether depreciation always helps.
questions.fix: Show demand shifting left or supply shifting right, label the exchange rate axis, then evaluate.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: A full range of marks was seen, with a pleasing number of high marks.
About 50 per cent gained full marks on the PPC diagram in 1(b).
In 1(c) most earned the first mark, and a significant number the second.
Question 5(a) was generally answered quite well, and many used the point about few natural resources.
mistakes: In 1(a) saying the figures were negative, or that the deficit worsened, did not earn marks.
In 1(b) the most common error was shifting the PPC left instead of showing a point inside it.
In 1(d) and 1(e) answers were often general, so many reached only one mark.
In 2(b) shortages under a maximum price were often drawn but not explained.
In 3(b) most described the four factors of production instead of judging whether encouraging entrepreneurs was the best route to long run growth.
In 4(b) answers often listed types of protection with no clear link to cutting the deficit.
fix: Use economic terms with the data: both years were in deficit, and the deficit grew.
Show unused labour as a point inside the PPC.
Always say why: why a shortage forms, why a policy lowers AD, why that cuts inflation.
Long run growth means a rise in potential output and LRAS, not short run growth from AD.
Make your judgement compare the strongest points on each side.

questions.issue: Some copied the negative figures or used the word worsened.
questions.fix: Say both years show a deficit, then say the deficit increased.

questions.issue: Shifting the curve left earned one mark, and labels like P and Q earned none.
questions.fix: Label the axes with two goods and mark a point inside the curve.

questions.issue: The third mark was rare, and valid evaluation was quite rare.
questions.fix: Cover the higher fuel price, its spread to other prices, why it may last such as a wage price spiral, then judge the extent.

questions.topic: Supply-side policy to diversify Nigeria's economy
questions.issue: Policies were vague and links to diversification were thin.
questions.fix: Name specific supply-side policies, explain strengths and weaknesses for diversification, then reach a balanced judgement.

questions.topic: Consumer surplus when higher costs raise price
questions.issue: Definitions were vague, diagrams poorly labelled, and most reached 4 at most.
questions.fix: Explain the role of PED in percentage terms, and show it on an accurate diagram.

questions.topic: Maximum price on food against transfer payments
questions.issue: Shortages, queues and illegal markets were asserted, not explained.
questions.fix: Explain that the lower price weakens producers' incentive to supply, and treat diagrams as support for your words.

questions.issue: Absolute advantage was defined vaguely, and tables and diagrams went unexplained.
questions.fix: Define absolute advantage as more output from the same resources, and note a country can have comparative advantage when another has absolute advantage in both.

questions.topic: Whether monetary policy is the only way to control inflation
questions.issue: Links between policy and inflation were asserted, and evaluation was general.
questions.fix: Explain why monetary policy cuts AD and inflation and how supply-side policy eases costs, then judge which works best.

papers.title: AS Level data response and essays
well: In 1(a) many gained the second mark for the 36 per cent calculation.
In 1(b) better answers linked one reason to the fall in doughnut sales for 2 marks.
Question 2(a) was generally answered quite well, with YED explained through a formula.
In 2(a) the size and sign of the coefficient were often analysed well with suitable examples.
mistakes: In 1(a) most missed the first mark for using the right figures in the right currency.
In 1(c) some called demand income elastic, ignoring the extract, and others could not say why it was inelastic.
In 1(d) very few mentioned information failure, and most wrote only about health.
In 1(e) there was little use of a diagram to show the effect on price and quantity.
In 3(b) a significant minority appeared to have no understanding of buffer stocks.
Very few attempted question 4, and most who did seemed unclear on money flows and the role of an open economy.
fix: Quote the data with its currency before you calculate.
Use the extract as evidence. If purchases held up when incomes fell, demand is income inelastic.
Explain a demerit good as overconsumed because of information failure.
Break part (a) essays into knowledge of the terms, analysis and evaluation.
Revise the circular flow in an open economy. The report calls it a new area and expects more questions on it.

questions.topic: Percentage change in the value of US doughnut sales
questions.issue: Many got the 36 per cent but not the mark for the right figures and currency.
questions.fix: Write the two values from the chart with their currency, then calculate.

questions.topic: Income elasticity of demand for doughnuts
questions.issue: Only a minority used the extract fully for 2 marks.
questions.fix: Say demand is income inelastic, and support it with the extract: people kept buying when incomes fell.

questions.issue: Most answers were vague and about health.
questions.fix: Say consumers underestimate the harm because of information failure, so the good is overconsumed.

questions.topic: Effect of an advert ban on the sugary food market
questions.issue: Most got only 1 or 2 marks, with little use of a diagram.
questions.fix: Shift demand left on a diagram, show the new price and quantity, and judge using PED.

questions.topic: Effects of the ban on consumers and government
questions.issue: Many were general, and some repeated 1(e).
questions.fix: Give one benefit and one drawback for consumers and for the government, then weigh them.

questions.topic: PED and changes in consumer surplus
questions.issue: Answers were often assertive and rarely passed Level 2.
questions.fix: Explain PED as the relative percentage change in quantity to a change in price, then show the surplus change on a diagram.

questions.issue: Few showed clear knowledge of merit goods with examples.
questions.fix: Explain underconsumption and information failure, why the private sector underprovides, then why intervention may fail.

questions.topic: Infrastructure investment and the circular flow
questions.issue: Investment was seen as an injection but rarely explained, and evaluation was not seen.
questions.fix: Explain investment as an injection, then judge it against the balance of injections and leakages.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Questions 9, 11, 13, 17, 19, 21, 24, 27 and 28 were answered correctly by 75 per cent or more.
mistakes: Questions 2, 6, 7 and 10 were answered correctly by fewer than 40 per cent.
In question 2, 42 per cent chose D without noticing that consumer 3 ended up with fewer goods.
In question 7, 37 per cent chose D, although AVC falls whenever MC is below it.
fix: A Pareto improvement needs at least one person better off and nobody worse off.
In the short run a firm must cover variable cost, and in the long run all its costs.
Net social benefit is total benefit minus total social cost.

questions.issue: 38 per cent chose the key A, and 42 per cent chose D.
questions.fix: Check every consumer. In option A consumer 3 gains and nobody loses.

questions.topic: Short run and long run shutdown
questions.issue: 30 per cent chose the key B, and 40 per cent chose C.
questions.fix: Firms X and Y cover variable cost but not total cost, so they stay open in the short run and close in the long run.

questions.topic: Marginal cost and average variable cost
questions.issue: 38 per cent chose the key B, and 37 per cent chose D.
questions.fix: While MC is below AVC, AVC is falling, whether MC itself is rising or falling.

questions.issue: Only 32 per cent chose the key B, and the rest split 21, 19 and 28 per cent across A, C and D.
questions.fix: Total benefit is x + z + w and total social cost is y + z + w, which leaves x minus y.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Questions 6, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27 and 29 were answered correctly by 80 per cent or more.
mistakes: Questions 4 and 9 were answered correctly by fewer than 45 per cent.
In question 4, 41 per cent chose B, possibly thinking of the short run.
In question 9, 28 per cent chose A, saying a sole supplier achieves no type of efficiency.
fix: In the long run a firm must cover average total cost, not just average variable cost.
A large profit making sole supplier can afford new processes, so think about dynamic efficiency.
Read the time period in each question before you choose.

questions.issue: 31 per cent chose the key C, and 41 per cent chose B.
questions.fix: In the long run average revenue must cover average total cost, so read the shutdown point from ATC, not AVC.

questions.issue: 43 per cent chose the key B, and 28 per cent chose A.
questions.fix: Expect dynamic efficiency but neither productive nor allocative efficiency.

questions.issue: One of the best answered questions, at 80 per cent or more.
questions.fix: Remember that benefits such as national pride are hard to value in money.

papers.title: A Level multiple choice
well: Questions 9, 11, 13, 17, 19, 21, 24, 26, 27 and 29 were answered correctly by 60 per cent or more.
mistakes: Questions 6 and 15 were answered correctly by fewer than 25 per cent.
In question 6, 51 per cent chose C.
In question 15 answers were spread across all four options, which may point to guessing.
fix: Check each firm twice: revenue against variable cost for the short run, then against total cost for the long run.
Learn that the demand for labour comes from the marginal revenue product.
Test each firm against both conditions before you choose.

questions.topic: Short run and long run shutdown
questions.issue: 23 per cent chose the key B, and 51 per cent chose C.
questions.fix: W and Z fail even the variable cost test. X and Y pass it but fall short of total cost, so they leave only in the long run.

questions.issue: One of the best answered questions, at 60 per cent or more.
questions.fix: An external cost falls on a third party, such as road congestion.

questions.issue: Only 20 per cent chose the key D, and the rest were spread across A, B and C.
questions.fix: Multiply the marginal physical product by marginal revenue to get the MRP curve.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: The good answers on this paper were balanced, well organised, tied to the question and backed by examples.
Question 3 drew some good balanced answers that covered the producer, the consumer and society.
Better answers on question 3 used real examples and applied a model, usually third degree price discrimination.
Most could explain what a budget surplus is in question 4, and some correctly linked falling AD to unemployment.
mistakes: In 1(a) few explained what a concentration ratio shows about competition, and many only added up the sales of the largest firms.
In 1(b) some wrote about consumption instead of production affecting a third party, and surprisingly few gave an example.
In 1(d) many drew MC without cutting AC at its lowest point, and a number gave no concluding remark.
In question 2 many did not link education as a merit good to positive externalities and allocative efficiency.
In question 4 many believed the government earns revenue from exports, and in question 5 production and productivity were often confused.
fix: Define a concentration ratio as the combined market share of a stated number of the largest firms, and say what it shows about competition.
On a monopoly diagram, draw MC through the lowest point of AC.
Draw a relevant diagram even when the question does not ask for one, such as price discrimination in question 3 or AD/AS in question 4.
Up to 6 marks are for evaluation, so develop and support your judgement.
Answer the exact question: in question 5 keep the focus on productivity, not GDP in general.

questions.issue: Answers were vague on meaning, and many stopped at adding up the top firms' sales.
questions.fix: Two marks are for what it shows about competition and two for the calculation: add the market shares of the named number of biggest firms.

questions.topic: Whether neither producer nor consumer pays for negative externalities
questions.issue: Some focused on consumption or on taxes, and few gave an example.
questions.fix: Define a negative externality as a cost to a third party, and give an example from production.

questions.issue: A number wrote generally about lack of competition instead of two reasons from the text.
questions.fix: Take two reasons from the article, other than negative externalities, and describe each.

questions.issue: Many drew the monopoly diagram inaccurately, and allocative efficiency was less known than productive efficiency.
questions.fix: Draw a labelled monopoly diagram with MC through minimum AC, and end with a conclusion on whether theory supports the article.

questions.issue: Most only argued that prices would rise, and a missing diagram ruled out Level 3.
questions.fix: Show the subsidy on a diagram and link merit goods, positive externalities and allocative efficiency.

questions.issue: Weaker answers treated it as simply charging higher prices and ignored the conditions.
questions.fix: State the conditions, use a third degree model, and judge the effects on producer, consumer and society.

questions.topic: Budget surplus, unemployment and the current account
questions.issue: Balance of payments effects were weakly applied, and few analysed the long run links.
questions.fix: Explain the short run AD effect on jobs, then analyse step by step how the surplus affects the current account over time.

questions.topic: Productivity and living standards in low income countries
questions.issue: Production and productivity were mixed up, and low income countries were described only by low GDP.
questions.fix: Stay on productivity and weigh issues such as FDI, income distribution, health and education, and how hard the gains are to measure.

papers.title: A Level data response and essays
well: The level of English was high, and many answers were of a high standard.
1(b) was relatively well answered, with correct PPC or AD/AS diagrams.
Most scored four or more in 1(d) by using the text to explain the benefits.
Question 2 produced some strong answers, especially where externalities were explained with a labelled diagram.
mistakes: In 1(a) few understood purchasing power parity or how a bundle of goods leads to an exchange rate.
In 1(c) fewer explained the standard of living, and the Gini coefficient caused the most trouble.
Question 3 answers suggested only part of the question was read, and few linked MES to market structure.
Weaker answers to question 4 left out the low income country part, and weaker answers to question 5 discussed expansionary policy.
Poorly drawn diagrams, diagrams never referred to and learned by heart answers that missed the question came up again.
fix: Use the data or text wherever it is relevant, because this is a data response paper.
Explain actual growth as a movement towards the PPC and potential growth as an outward shift.
A rising Gini coefficient means income is spread less evenly.
Develop each evaluative point so it reaches level 2 evaluation.
Write a relevant, concise answer. Long answers were often poorly directed.

questions.issue: Few showed understanding of the term.
questions.fix: Compare the cost of the same bundle of goods in two currencies, and turn that into an exchange rate.

questions.topic: BRI and Pakistan's actual and potential growth
questions.issue: Some drew correct diagrams but could not explain the difference.
questions.fix: Show a move from inside to the PPC for actual growth and an outward shift for potential growth.

questions.topic: Standard of living in Pakistan and China, 2014 to 2018
questions.issue: Most used the data, but fewer explained what the standard of living means.
questions.fix: Define the standard of living, then use GDP per head, unemployment and the Gini coefficient to judge the change.

questions.topic: Long run impact of the BRI
questions.issue: Only the best answers saw limits as well as benefits.
questions.fix: Use the article for benefits to each country, then weigh the limitations.

questions.issue: Many made only level 1 evaluative comments.
questions.fix: Explain the reduced negative externality on a referenced diagram, analyse two policies the same way, and develop your evaluation.

questions.fix: Link economies of scale to MES, compare MES with market demand, then evaluate which structure results.

questions.topic: Depreciation and growth in a low income country
questions.issue: Weaker answers covered only the depreciation.
questions.fix: Analyse exports, imports and GDP with AD/AS, then evaluate the outcome for a low income country.

questions.topic: Monetary policy against inflation and other aims
questions.issue: Weaker answers were descriptive or discussed expansionary policy.
questions.fix: Use contractionary policy, cover consumer demand and investment, then assess the effect on other macroeconomic aims.
